articles.title: One Developer, Five Roles
articles.description: I finished a feature last week. It worked. I felt good.  Then a small voice said, "Did you check it...
articles.body_html:
I finished a feature last week. It worked. I felt good.

Then a small voice said, "Did you check it on your phone?"

Another voice said, "It's fine. Just ship it."

Both voices were mine.

I'm a freelance developer, and I work alone. When something needs doing, there is nobody to give it to. The word "developer" is on my profile. But that is only one of my jobs.

I read a post here by xulingfeng. It says every part of a company helps the others, and also pushes back on them. I liked that.

The Third Cup: Five Elements, One IT Company
Readers love the cozy café narrative framing
xulingfeng
xulingfeng
for The Third Cup
Nov 22

The Third Cup: Five Elements, One IT Company

#discuss #management #career #programming
93 reactions Comments 53 comments
7 min read

In a company, people argue in a meeting. When you work alone, the argument happens in your head.

So here are the five people who live in mine.

🎨 1. The Designer

The designer says, "That button is two pixels off."

Fine. I fix it.

Then, "The heading looks too heavy." Okay. Then, "Let's add a small animation."

The designer is usually right. The page does look better. But "better" never ends, and the deadline does.

So I ask one thing:

Will the visitor notice this, or am I just being picky?

Sometimes it is worth it. I just want to know before I spend the hour.

💻 2. The Developer

This one loves to build.


Give him a problem and he already has ten tabs open. He cannot wait to start.

But he starts too fast. A client once said, "I need a dashboard." I thought of charts and filters. They wanted a simple list with a search box.

Now I ask, "What will you do on this screen?" It takes five minutes. It saves a whole weekend.

🧪 3. The Tester


Nobody invites the tester. He comes anyway.

  • "What if the form is empty?"
  • "What if someone taps Submit twice?"
  • "What if the internet is slow?"

Testing your own work is hard. You already know how it should work, so your fingers take the easy path. A real visitor does not know that path.

So I act like a person in a rush. Small screen. Wrong input. Back button. It feels silly. But it is better than the client finding the bug first.

🚀 4. The Deployer


"It works on my machine."

We all say it. But the client does not have my machine.

I use Vercel or Railway, and they help a lot. But they cannot know what I forgot. If I forgot an environment variable, it is still missing.

So I am not done when the build turns green. I am done when I open the live link and click through it like a stranger.

📩 5. The Support Person


The message always starts the same way:

"Hi, just one small thing..."

Sometimes it really is small. A typo. A phone number.

Sometimes "one small thing" is a whole login system.

This person has to stay polite, understand the real request, and give the time and price before saying yes. Saying "sure, no problem" is easy. The developer pays for it later.

Now I say this instead:

"Sure, let me check what it needs. I'll tell you the time and cost first."

Nobody feels turned down, and I don't promise anything blind.

The five roles at a glance

Role What they want What they forget
Designer Make it look better The deadline
Developer Start building now To ask what is needed
Tester Break it before users do That time is short
Deployer Check the live site That it "worked locally"
Support Keep the client happy To say the cost first

When they fight

This is the hard part of working alone.

The designer wants one more day. Support already promised Friday. The tester found a bug. The developer says, "It's rare. Ignore it."

It happened to me on a small shop site. I wanted to fix the spacing on the product page. But I had told the client "Friday." On Thursday night I opened the site on a small phone. The checkout button was half hidden.

I fixed the button and left the spacing alone. We launched on Friday. The client never noticed the spacing.

Now I check the phone view before I polish anything. Things that break go first. Things that only look nicer can wait.

What helps me

I can't hire four more people. But I can stop them from talking all at once.

My simple checklist
  • Before I start: write a few lines about what "done" means.
  • While I build: let the developer work. Put shiny ideas on a list for later.
  • Before I ship: switch hats on purpose. Check phone view, empty fields, wrong input, env variables.
  • After I ship: open the live site and use it from start to end.
  • When a new request comes: check first, then answer.

None of this is smart or new. The hard part is doing it at the end of a long day, when "it's probably fine" sounds so believable.

One desk, five chairs


Working alone does not mean I am great at five jobs. It means I try to notice which job needs me right now, and let the quiet ones speak before the loud ones take over.

So I keep asking myself one thing:

Which chair am I sitting in right now?

Your turn ☕

If you work alone, or you are the whole tech team: which role do you skip first when the deadline is close?

Did it ever hurt you later? Tell me in the comments. I would love to hear it.

articles.title: What If Every AI Model Was a Pokémon? I Built It.
articles.description: Every week, there's a new AI model.  GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek... and then comes Pro, Flash,...
articles.body_html:
Every week, there's a new AI model.

GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek... and then comes Pro, Flash, Mini, Lite, and so on.

Keeping track of all these models can get a little overwhelming.

Most AI comparison websites show the same thing: tables, charts, benchmark scores, and pricing.

They're useful, but I wanted to make exploring AI models a little more fun.

So I thought, what if AI models were Pokémon?

That's how ModelDex was born.

What is ModelDex?

ModelDex is an interactive Pokédex for AI models, bringing together 690+ benchmarked AI models and 1,025 Pokémon species.

It covers text, image, video, speech, audio, transcription, and music generation models.

Each eligible AI model gets a unique Pokémon based on its actual capabilities, intelligence, speed, and other measured metrics—plus you can filter by Pokémon Type, Generation (Gen 1–9), Class (Mythical / Legendary / Standard), Provider, or Open weights.

  • Try it live: https://model-dex.vercel.app/

How does the matching work?

I didn't want to randomly assign Pokémon to AI models. I wanted every match to have a transparent, mathematical reason behind it.

ModelDex uses real benchmark and model data from Artificial Analysis, OpenRouter, Design Arena, and PokéAPI.

Pokémon have six base stats, mapped directly to measured AI dimensions:

Pokémon stat AI capability
HP Context window and maximum output
Attack Coding and engineering
Defense Legal and cybersecurity
Special Attack Core intelligence / arena power index
Special Defense Healthcare, modalities, and visual arenas
Speed Output speed (tokens/s) and response time

Model families (like Flash-Lite → Flash → Pro or Haiku → Sonnet → Opus) also align onto multi-stage Pokémon evolution lines, while provider signatures give subtle type leanings (for example, reasoning models lean Psychic and coding models lean Electric).

Every assignment is unique 1-to-1, and clicking any card shows exactly why a model received its Pokémon.

One strict rule: if a model doesn't have benchmark data, it stays unassigned.

No made-up scores.

Not every model can be legendary

The matching engine also enforces strict tier guardrails:

  • Powerful models (Power ≥ 75) cannot receive weak, baby, or unevolved Pokémon.
  • Lightweight models (Power < 40) cannot receive strong, Legendary, or Mythical Pokémon.
  • As newer and stronger AI models arrive, stale locks can automatically release so older models don't hold top Legendaries forever.

Interestingly, Mewtwo and Mew are still unclaimed at the time of writing.

Maybe the next generation of AI models will finally catch them.

Built with simplicity in mind

I wanted to keep the project simple, fast, and free to run.

The application is built using:

  • Next.js, React, and TypeScript
  • Static site generation with automated twice-weekly data refreshes
  • Upstream benchmark and Pokédex data from Artificial Analysis, OpenRouter, Design Arena, and PokéAPI

Just open the website and start exploring.

Give it a try

I really enjoyed building this side project because it combines three things I enjoy: AI, development, and creative data visualization.

Sometimes we don't need more raw spreadsheets—just a more fun way to explore them.

Try it live: https://model-dex.vercel.app/

I'd love to hear your feedback and suggestions. Which Pokémon did your favorite AI model get?

Thanks to Artificial Analysis, OpenRouter, Design Arena, and PokéAPI for their data and platforms.

All Pokémon characters, names, and artwork belong to their respective rights holders. Attribution or takedown requests: modeldex.app@gmail.com.

articles.title: Native WebMCP or a Polyfill? Build a Comparison You Can Trust
articles.description: A React demo exposes a tool, an inspector discovers it, and a call returns the expected event title....
articles.body_html:
A React demo exposes a tool, an inspector discovers it, and a call returns the expected event title. That is a useful milestone. It does not tell you which implementation made the result possible.

This distinction matters when a fallback quietly installs itself before the application starts. A successful demo can then become a misleading browser compatibility claim. For a project such as Trip Workbench, where the same workflow is useful to humans and agents, I want the application to keep working while the evidence remains specific.

The companion example separates native WebMCP from the W3C OSS polyfill at bootstrap. Its purpose is to compare one small application contract without pretending the implementations are interchangeable.

Start with two explicit execution paths

The current WebMCP draft is still evolving. The polyfill provides an implementation of selected browser-facing capabilities; it does not turn every browser into a native WebMCP browser.

The first design decision is therefore outside React. Select an execution path before rendering components or registering tools:

const contextBeforeSetup = document.modelContext;

if (lane === "polyfill") {
  installPolyfill();
}

const context = document.modelContext;
if (!context?.registerTool || !context.getTools || !context.executeTool) {
  throw new Error("Required WebMCP methods are unavailable");
}

This is an abbreviated view of bootstrap.ts. The native path never installs a fallback. If it cannot provide the methods the example needs, it fails visibly.

The polyfill path records whether a context existed before installation. That detail prevents another overclaim: an existing context is not automatically native. An extension, test harness, or earlier application script might have created it. The fixture reports provenance as “pre-existing” or “installed by this fixture,” leaving browser identity to the run record.

Define the comparison before running it

Use one read-only event summary tool with fixed synthetic data. Keep its name, input schema, callback, and expected output identical in both paths. Avoid comparing a native declarative form against an imperative polyfill tool and calling the result an implementation comparison.

The useful questions are narrow:

Question How to establish it
Did the expected tool register? Inspect discovery after mounting
Does a valid call return the fixture? Execute the same arguments
Does invalid input fail safely? Exercise application validation
Does unmounting remove the registration? Inspect discovery after cleanup
Which implementation supplied the context? Record setup order and browser configuration

A green result on this table says something meaningful about the tested application. It says little about untested platform features, cross-frame behavior, or browser permission enforcement.

Keep lifecycle behavior in the experiment

The browser fixture mounts a React component that exposes read_event_summary. A button removes that component. This creates a simple lifecycle test: the tool should exist while its owner is mounted and disappear when that owner leaves.

React's effect documentation makes cleanup part of the contract. Development Strict Mode also exercises setup and cleanup more than a simple production mount. That is a useful way to find registration leaks, provided the test records which build it ran.

Do not “fix” duplicate tools by removing Strict Mode from the experiment. First check whether registration has a matching cleanup operation and whether the component uses a stable tool identity. The companion uses the pinned React hook package for this lifecycle and keeps the bootstrap choice outside that component.

The unit tests focus on the bootstrap guarantees: the native path cannot call the installer, explicit installation has recorded provenance, a partial context is rejected, and a missing native context does not silently change the experiment. These tests passed locally. They are not native-browser conformance tests.

Compare documented limitations separately

The polyfill's own testing notes are a better starting point than a generic “works everywhere” label. They distinguish supported behavior from platform features JavaScript cannot fully reproduce.

Three boundaries affect application design. Declarative forms are a separate capability; do not infer them from successful imperative registration. Script-created events cannot acquire the browser's trusted-event status. Permission behavior also has limitations when the implementation cannot inspect or enforce native policy information.

The installer preserves an existing context, including a partial one. Installing it again is therefore not a general repair strategy. If a method your application requires is absent, report the missing capability and keep the human workflow usable.

These are documented differences, not performance measurements from this example. A useful comparison keeps those categories separate rather than presenting a single percentage called “compatibility.”

Reproduce the small test first

The package pins its dependencies and includes a lockfile. From its code directory:

npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
npm run serve

Open the fixture with the requested execution path in a dedicated browser profile. Record the browser version, operating system, WebMCP feature configuration, initial context presence, and tool discovery before and after unmounting. Run the native path without loading the fallback. Run the fallback path in an environment where the fixture can actually install it; otherwise record that the existing implementation was preserved.

Native browser execution remains a separate step in this package. The included result sheet intentionally leaves those observations unfilled until a compatible browser run is completed. That is preferable to promoting unit-test results into browser evidence.

Use the fallback to support a product decision

The comparison becomes useful when it answers a specific deployment question. Perhaps the application needs imperative read tools today and can keep ordinary form submission for users. Perhaps it depends on native declarative behavior and should show a capability-specific enhancement only in eligible browsers.

Either decision is stronger than treating one global property as proof of complete support. Keep capability checks close to the features that need them, record the implementation used in reproducible runs, and let the existing UI remain the dependable path through the application.

A small, honest comparison is easier to maintain as WebMCP changes. More importantly, readers can rerun it and understand exactly what a passing result establishes.

articles.title: Why Does Vite Run on localhost:5173? It's Not Random!
articles.description: React project run on localhost:3000.  Then you start a Vite project, and suddenly it's...
articles.body_html:
React project run on localhost:3000.

Then you start a Vite project, and suddenly it's localhost:5173. 🤔

Why such a random number? I finally looked it up, and it's not random at all.

🏢 First, what is a port?

Think of your computer as an apartment building.

In real life On your computer
The building localhost (your own machine)
A flat number The port
The person living there Your running app

So localhost:5173 simply means:

"Go to my building and knock on flat 5173."

🕵️ The secret hidden in 5173

Squint a little and read it like this:

Number Letter Why
5 V Roman numeral for 5
1 I Looks like I
7 T Looks like T
3 E A flipped E

5173 = VITE ⚡

It's like a personalised number plate. At first you see digits, then you spot the name, and you can't unsee it.

🔄 Vite used to live at 3000

Here's the part I didn't know: earlier versions of Vite used port 3000 too.

In Vite 3, the team changed the default to 5173 to move away from such a commonly used port.

Imagine flat 3000 is the most popular flat in the building. Many tools want to move in, but for a given address, only one can live there at a time. So Vite packed its bags and moved to a flat with its own name on it. 📦

Why was 3000 picked in the first place? I couldn't find a confirmed reason.

It's like a popular hangout spot. People keep going there because everyone already knows it.

😵 Why am I seeing 5174?

Sometimes your project opens on 5174 instead.

That means flat 5173 is already occupied, often by another Vite project you left running in a different terminal.

By default, Vite knocks on the next door:

5173 ❌ occupied
5174 ✅ free, moving in!

If 5174 is busy too, it keeps looking.

🛠️ Want to choose the port yourself?

In vite.config.js:

import { defineConfig } from 'vite'

export default defineConfig({
  // keep your existing plugins here
  server: {
    port: 3000,
    strictPort: true,
  },
})
  • port: the flat you want
  • strictPort: true: "This flat or nothing!" Vite stops with an error instead of trying the next one

Or do it just once from the terminal:

npm run dev -- --port 3000

🎯 Quick recap

  • 🏢 A port is like a flat number
  • ⚡ 5173 can be read as VITE
  • 📦 Vite 3 moved the default from 3000 to 5173
  • 🚪 5174 usually appears because 5173 is busy

Happy Coding :)

articles.title: How I built Casthop, an open-source live studio in the browser
articles.description: I wanted a StreamYard-style studio I could run myself, and I couldn't find a good open-source one. So...
articles.body_html:
I wanted a StreamYard-style studio I could run myself, and I couldn't find a good open-source one. So I built Casthop.

Casthop is a live studio that runs in the browser. You sign in as the host, send guests a link (they don't need an account), put up to six people on stage, and send one mix to as many RTMP destinations as you want. While you're live you can clip the last 30 or 60 seconds, add a 9:16 output next to the 16:9, and record each person on their own track. YouTube, Twitch and Kick chat land in one place, and you can pin a comment on the video.

It's licensed AGPL-3.0. Self-hosting is free. The first public release, v0.1.0, came out on 27 November 2026.

The people in the screenshots were made for these shots.

How it's put together

The media path is LiveKit, Egress, Redis and an RTMP server. Those run in Docker on your machine. The app is a Cloudflare Worker with Durable Objects and D1. Stream keys stay in Durable Object storage and are never sent back to guests. The audio and video hot paths — noise suppression and the compositor — are Rust compiled to WebAssembly.

That split is the whole design. The Worker owns rooms, guests and "go live." The media servers do the heavy lifting.

Three problems that showed up once it was running

The 9:16 compositor was dying on first start

When you go live with a vertical destination, Casthop starts a second compositor for 9:16, next to the 16:9 one. The watch path gives a new compositor a short start grace, so a first heartbeat isn't treated as already gone.

That grace was only wired to the 16:9 egress id. On a cold first go-live, a watch that ran before the portrait compositor had joined treated it as dead and stopped it with "Compositor left." An earlier bug made this worse: the start path wrote a fake heartbeat, so a compositor that hadn't loaded yet looked stale in a three-second window, got restarted, and sometimes two portrait compositors ended up publishing to the same RTMP URL.

The start grace now covers the 9:16 egress too, the heartbeat is only set by a real beat, and a restart stops any extra portrait compositor in the room. That's #102 and #113.

One client could fill the studio's sockets

Studio state goes out over WebSockets: stage changes, chat, and, while you're live, a full public state at least once a second. We capped a room at 256 sockets, which is well above a real studio. The upgrade itself was still unauthenticated, and guests do need to connect before they have a session. One client could open all 256, and every real host or viewer after that got a 503.

The Worker now stamps each upgrade with the client network — an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /64 — and ignores a caller-supplied header. A ninth open socket from that network gets a 429. The 256 room cap stays as a backstop. That's #114, after the room cap in #99.

Two uploads could land on the same R2 key

Per-person recordings upload media in chunks to R2. The route used to validate with the studio, write the object, then ask the studio to count the bytes. Validation reserved nothing, so two PUTs to the same index both passed and both wrote to the same key. Only one was counted; the other got a 409, but its object stayed. A 1-byte body and an 8 MiB body to the same index could leave 8 MiB stored while only 1 byte counted toward the caps.

The upload now reserves that index for 20 seconds, with the byte count and a nonce. A second upload in flight gets 429, and the recorder already retries 429. If the R2 put fails, the Worker aborts and frees the index for a retry. Commit and abort both need the matching nonce and byte count. That's #80.

A related limit bit us on sign-in mail. The rate limits used the raw CF-Connecting-IP. One IPv6 host usually holds a whole /64, so each source address counted as a new client. Four addresses in one /64 could send a dozen real sign-in mails to one inbox, where a single client is allowed three. Limits now group IPv6 by /64, and one inbox can get at most 20 sign-in mails per 15 minutes, then at most one more per minute. That's #86.

Running it locally

You need Linux, Docker, and Bun 1.4.5 or newer. Do not use npm.

git clone https://github.com/casthop/casthop.git && cd casthop
cp .env.example .env
cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
mkdir -p data/recordings data/rtmp && chmod 777 data/recordings
docker compose up -d
bun install
bun run dev

The sign-in link is printed in the terminal (no email is sent locally). Open http://127.0.0.1:5173, create a studio, copy the guest link, and press Go live. Default destinations are local test servers, so nothing goes public. Step-by-step docs are at casthop.com.

What's still rough

Guests on strict networks may have a hard time until NAT traversal is better, and there's no X or LinkedIn chat yet. Expect other rough edges; this is an early release.

The repo is github.com/casthop/casthop.

articles.title: I built a webhook inspector with replay and mocks, and almost shipped three security bugs
articles.description: Every developer who has integrated Stripe or GitHub webhooks knows the loop: trigger an event, squint...
articles.body_html:
Every developer who has integrated Stripe or GitHub webhooks knows the loop:
trigger an event, squint at logs, guess what the payload looked like, tweak the
handler, trigger again.

Hosted inspectors fix that, but your payloads (often with customer data) sit on
someone else's server. So I built Hookpit, a self-hostable webhook
inspector with replay and mock responses.

What it does

  • One click gives you a capture URL; requests show up live
  • The raw body is stored exactly as sent
  • Replay any request to your own app, editing it first
  • Mock responses: make the URL behave like a fake API, with path patterns, placeholders like {{uuid}}, a configurable delay, and binary bodies
  • Per-IP rate limiting on replay and capture, with 429 and Retry-After

Four things I learned

1. Don't let the framework "help" with bodies. Express parses JSON and
throws away the original bytes. For an inspector (and for signature checks) you
need the raw body, so I disabled the parser on the capture route and wrote a
test with deliberately odd JSON.

2. Replay is an SSRF machine unless you stop it. Replay makes your server
fetch a URL a user typed. Type http://169.254.169.254/ on a cloud host and
you may read the instance's credentials. I blocked private and reserved
addresses (including IPv6-wrapped IPv4 like ::ffff:127.0.0.1), refused
redirects, and checked the address inside the DNS lookup used for the real
connection, so DNS rebinding can't swap it afterwards.

3. Mocks let users make your server say anything. That means stored XSS
(an HTML mock served from your origin), header injection (%0d%0a in a query
string ending up in a header), and template tricks ({{constructor}}). My
answers: force Content-Security-Policy: sandbox on every mock response, never
template headers, allow only plain property lookups in bodies, and cap how much
a template can expand.

4. Prove your tests can fail. For each protection I temporarily broke it and
watched the tests go red: 13 failures with SSRF protection off, 15 with header
validation off, 4 with prototype access allowed. A test that has never failed
might not test anything.

A bonus bug that only my laptop could find

CI was green, but docker compose up failed on my Apple Silicon Mac:
better-sqlite3 has no prebuilt binary for Node 20 on ARM Linux, so it tried to
compile and the slim image had no compiler. GitHub's runners are x86, so CI
could never see it. Fix: a build stage with the toolchain, copying only the
result into a slim final image.

The open-source part

Within days of posting the first good-first-issues, two strangers sent pull
requests, and both are merged: rate limiting, and binary mock bodies. I ran each
branch locally before merging. Reviewing taught me as much as writing the code:
I asked for a small test-cleanup fix in one, and in the other I found a gap in
the limiter (creating many endpoints sidesteps the per-endpoint limit), which is
now a public issue.

Try it 


bash
git clone https://github.com/Aliweb789/hookpit.git
cd hookpit
docker compose up --build

articles.title: Building ROOTS: Bringing India's 36 Cultural Regions to Life with Cloudinary, Generative AI & Next.js
articles.description: Every place has a story. Every story deserves to be felt.   28 States. 8 Union Territories....
articles.body_html:
Every place has a story. Every story deserves to be felt.

28 States. 8 Union Territories. Countless Traditions. One Soul.

India is not simply a geographical destination. It is a collection of languages, traditions, childhood memories, architectural wonders, festivals, flavors, and stories passed down through generations.

But what if technology could bring these experiences together in a single digital space?

What if cultural heritage could be explored, transformed, personalized, and carried home as a digital memory?

That question became the inspiration behind ROOTS — The Soul of India, an immersive digital cultural museum built for the Cloudinary "Celebrate Where You're From" Mini-Hackathon.

🌐 Experience ROOTS

💻 Explore the GitHub Repository

🏛️ The Vision Behind ROOTS

Most cultural websites present information through static photographs, descriptions, and conventional galleries.

ROOTS takes a different approach.

Instead of simply telling visitors about a place, it invites them to experience its identity.

The goal was to build a digital museum where technology complements cultural storytelling rather than overshadowing it.

Every regional exhibition, photographic transformation, interactive experience, and personalized keepsake contributes to one central idea:

Heritage deserves more than preservation. It deserves to be experienced.

✨ Exploring the ROOTS Experience

1. Cinematic Museum Entrance

The experience begins with a cinematic introduction designed to establish an emotional connection with India's cultural heritage.

Rather than resembling a conventional dashboard, the interface draws inspiration from elegant museum exhibitions, editorial typography, and cultural archives.

2. Interactive Cultural Atlas

ROOTS brings together all 28 Indian states and 8 union territories within a unified cultural atlas.

Each regional exhibition explores:

  • Traditional cuisine
  • Cultural clothing and textiles
  • Indigenous childhood games
  • Festivals and celebrations
  • Historical architecture
  • Regional traditions and heritage

Distinct regional color palettes help establish individual cultural identities while maintaining a cohesive museum experience.

3. A Journey Back Home

One of the signature storytelling experiences is a five-chapter journey:

  • The Land — Discover geographical and architectural identity.
  • The Taste — Explore traditional flavors.
  • The Celebration — Experience regional festivals.
  • The Memory — Rediscover childhood and cultural nostalgia.
  • The Keepsake — Carry a personalized digital memory forward.

The experience connects cultural discovery with emotion and belonging.

4. Archive Lens

Archive Lens introduces interactive historical and contemporary photographic comparisons.

Visitors can explore the relationship between India's architectural past and present through a comparison slider.

A dedicated heritage media registry organizes historical references, contemporary imagery, source information, attribution, and provenance metadata.

The design emphasizes an important distinction: authentic historical documentation and creatively transformed imagery should not be presented as interchangeable.

5. Halide Process Studio

Inspired by historical photographic techniques, the Halide Process Studio explores creative visual transformations using Cloudinary.

Visitors can experiment with archival aesthetics, monochromatic imagery, sepia tones, and photographic effects.

6. Generative AI Heritage Lab

The AI Heritage Lab explores the creative potential of Cloudinary's generative media capabilities.

Its transformation workflows include:

  • Generative image restoration
  • Intelligent image expansion
  • Creative photographic enhancement
  • Before-and-after comparisons

AI-generated modifications are intended as creative interpretations, not substitutes for authentic historical evidence.

7. Personalized Postcard Atelier

The Postcard Atelier turns cultural exploration into personal creation.

Visitors can personalize cultural imagery with messages and decorative elements, generating downloadable digital postcards through Cloudinary's media transformation pipeline.

Instead of leaving the museum with only information, visitors can leave with a personal keepsake.

8. Letter From Home & Cultural Passport

The Letter From Home experience explores the emotional connection between identity, memory, and belonging.

The Cultural Passport adds an interactive layer to regional exploration, allowing visitors to collect digital stamps as they discover different cultural regions.

☁️ Cloudinary: More Than an Image Hosting Platform

One of the most important architectural decisions behind ROOTS was to make Cloudinary a core part of the application rather than a supplementary image hosting service.

Cloudinary connects the visual, creative, and technical layers of the experience.

The project's media requirements included:

  • Delivering high-resolution cultural photography efficiently.
  • Supporting responsive media across devices.
  • Creating distinct regional visual identities.
  • Enabling historical photographic effects.
  • Integrating generative AI transformations.
  • Composing personalized downloadable postcards.
  • Supporting secure media processing.

Cloudinary provides the foundation for these workflows.

1. Intelligent Media Optimization

A digital museum spanning 36 cultural regions requires a substantial amount of visual content.

Serving original high-resolution images without optimization can create unnecessary bandwidth consumption and slower experiences.

ROOTS uses Cloudinary's automatic format and quality transformations:

f_auto,q_auto

f_auto allows Cloudinary to select an appropriate delivery format based on browser capabilities.

q_auto automatically adjusts image quality to balance visual fidelity and file size.

Combined with responsive resizing, these transformations help deliver visually rich cultural experiences across different devices.

2. Content-Aware Image Cropping

Cultural photographs often contain important architectural details, intricate textiles, and artistic compositions.

Conventional center cropping can remove meaningful visual elements.

Cloudinary's automatic gravity helps address this challenge:

c_fill,g_auto,w_1200,h_800

Content-aware cropping supports more intelligent framing while maintaining consistent exhibition layouts.
