articles.title: Reviewing AI‑generated C# before it hits production
articles.description: AI assistants now write a big share of the C# in our pull requests. The code compiles, the tests pass...
articles.body_html:
AI assistants now write a big share of the C# in our pull requests. The code compiles, the tests pass locally and the demo goes well. Then it reaches production and something breaks: a query times out, an endpoint leaks another customer's data, or the app runs out of sockets at peak load.

The problem isn't that AI writes bad code. It writes plausible code, tuned for the happy path it was shown. Production is where the unhappy paths live. This post covers the mistakes I see most often in AI-generated C#, why "works on my machine" keeps happening, and the checks I now run before anything ships.

What went wrong:

Each snippet below is the kind of code an assistant hands back when you ask for "an endpoint that does X". Every one of them works in a demo. For each, I cover why the assistant wrote it, what breaks in production, and how to catch it in review.

1. SQL built with string interpolation 

// AI-generated: works, and is injectable
var orders = await _db.Orders
    .FromSqlRaw($"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerName = '{name}'")
    .ToListAsync();

// Fix: FromSql turns the interpolated value into a SQL parameter (EF Core 7+)
var orders = await _db.Orders
    .FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerName = {name}")
    .ToListAsync();

Why the AI wrote it: FromSqlRaw with $"..." appears all over older blog posts and forum answers, so it is a high-probability completion. The interpolation looks like parameterization but isn't: the string is fully built before EF Core ever sees it. FromSql takes a FormattableString instead, so EF can turn each {value} into a real @p0 parameter.

What happens in prod: Any search box or query-string filter that reaches this code becomes an attack surface. A name like x' OR '1'='1 returns every customer's orders. If the database login has broad rights, '; DROP TABLE Orders;-- is far worse. Report filters, search screens and "export to Excel" endpoints are the usual victims, because they take free text.

Catch it in review: Search the diff for FromSqlRaw, ExecuteSqlRaw, SqlCommand and string concatenation near SQL keywords. Any user-supplied value inside the SQL string itself is an automatic reject. As a second line of defence, give the app's database login only the rights it needs, and never db_owner or sa in production.

2. No authorization or ownership check 

// AI-generated: any logged-in user can read any invoice by guessing IDs
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetInvoice(int id)
    => Ok(await _db.Invoices.FindAsync(id));

// Fix: require auth, scope to the caller, return a DTO instead of the entity
[Authorize]
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetInvoice(int id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var userId = User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
    var invoice = await _db.Invoices
        .Where(i => i.Id == id && i.OwnerId == userId)
        .Select(i => new InvoiceDto(i.Id, i.Amount, i.DueDate))
        .FirstOrDefaultAsync(ct);

    return invoice is null ? NotFound() : Ok(invoice);
}

Why the AI wrote it: You asked for "an endpoint that returns an invoice by ID", and that is exactly what you got. The assistant doesn't know your tenancy model, or that invoice 1043 belongs to a different client. It skips the ownership check because you never mentioned one.

What happens in prod: This is Broken Object Level Authorization, number one in the OWASP API Security Top 10. A logged-in user changes /invoices/1042 to /invoices/1043 and reads another company's billing. Returning the raw entity makes it worse, because internal notes, cost prices, audit fields and navigation properties all get serialized. With lazy loading switched on, one request can pull in half the object graph.

Catch it in review: Every action needs a clear answer to "who may call this, and for which records?" Look for FindAsync(id) with no user or tenant filter, and for actions that return EF entity types. In multi-tenant apps, a global query filter such as HasQueryFilter(i => i.TenantId == _tenant.Id) makes the safe path the default, so a forgotten Where doesn't leak data.

3. Blocking on async code 

// AI-generated
public IActionResult GetRates()
    => Ok(_rateService.GetRatesAsync().Result);

// Fix: async all the way down, with cancellation
public async Task<IActionResult> GetRates(CancellationToken ct)
    => Ok(await _rateService.GetRatesAsync(ct));

Why the AI wrote it: The assistant often writes a synchronous method first, then needs to call an async service from it. .Result is the shortest way to make it compile.

What happens in prod: In ASP.NET Core, the blocked call holds a thread-pool thread for the whole wait. One tester never notices. At 300 concurrent users the pool runs dry, the runtime adds threads only slowly, and response times jump from milliseconds to tens of seconds, even while the CPU sits idle. In classic ASP.NET or desktop apps it can deadlock outright because of the synchronization context. Its cousin async void is just as dangerous: an exception thrown inside it can crash the whole process instead of reaching your error handler.

Catch it in review: Search for .Result, .Wait(), .GetAwaiter().GetResult() and any async void that isn't an event handler. Check that CancellationToken flows from the action down to EF Core and HttpClient calls, so a cancelled request stops doing work instead of finishing a query nobody will read.

4. A new HttpClient per call 

// AI-generated
using var client = new HttpClient();
var json = await client.GetStringAsync(url);

// Fix: register once and inject; add a timeout and resilience
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<MarketDataClient>(c =>
{
    c.BaseAddress = new Uri(builder.Configuration["MarketData:BaseUrl"]!);
    c.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
})
.AddStandardResilienceHandler(); // Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience

Why the AI wrote it: Wrapping an IDisposable in using looks like textbook good practice, and the assistant applies the rule mechanically.

What happens in prod: HttpClient is designed to be reused. Each disposed instance leaves its socket in TIME_WAIT for a while after closing. A busy service calling a market-data or payment API runs out of ephemeral ports, and every outbound call fails with a SocketException. Switching to one static client fixes the sockets but caches DNS forever, which breaks when the dependency fails over to a new IP. IHttpClientFactory handles both problems. The default 100-second timeout hurts too: one hung dependency ties up your request threads for nearly two minutes.

Catch it in review: Flag any new HttpClient() in application code. Check that every typed client sets an explicit timeout. Make sure retry policies suit the calls they wrap; never blindly retry a payment or another call that isn't safe to repeat.

5. Filtering in memory instead of in the database 

// AI-generated: pulls the whole table, then filters
var open = _db.Trades.ToList().Where(t => t.Status == "Open").Take(50);

// Fix: let SQL do the work
var open = await _db.Trades
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(t => t.Status == "Open")
    .OrderByDescending(t => t.CreatedAt)
    .Take(50)
    .ToListAsync(ct);

Why the AI wrote it: ToList() is the classic "fix" for LINQ translation errors. When EF Core can't translate an expression, such as a custom C# method inside Where, the quickest workaround is to load everything and filter in memory. The code compiles and the error goes away.

What happens in prod: The dev database has 200 trades; production has 5 million. Every request now pulls the whole table over the network, tracks every entity, then throws away all but 50 rows. The result is slow pages, memory spikes, garbage-collection pauses and eventually timeouts or an OutOfMemoryException. The database also does far more I/O than it needs to, which slows every other query on the server.

Catch it in review: Look for ToList(), ToArray() or AsEnumerable() before Where, OrderBy or Take. Turn on EF Core's SQL logging in development and read the query it actually generates. Add AsNoTracking() to read-only queries, and always cap results with paging.

6. Swallowed exceptions 

// AI-generated
public async Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(int id)
{
    try
    {
        return await _db.Customers.FindAsync(id);
    }
    catch (Exception)
    {
        return null;
    }
}

// Fix: no blanket catch here; handle failures once, centrally
public Task<Customer?> GetCustomerAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct)
    => _db.Customers.FirstOrDefaultAsync(c => c.Id == id, ct);

// Program.cs: unhandled errors are logged and returned as ProblemDetails (500)
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();
app.UseExceptionHandler();

Why the AI wrote it: Assistants are tuned to hand back code that "doesn't crash". A blanket catch is the cheapest way to look robust.

What happens in prod: The database goes down, but the API returns 404 Not Found, because null means "no such customer". Nothing is logged as an error, so your alerts never fire. Support spends a day chasing "missing" customers who actually exist. When null can mean both "not found" and "broken", nobody can tell the two apart.

Catch it in review: Reject any catch (Exception) that neither rethrows nor logs. Allow catches only for specific exceptions the code can genuinely recover from, and let everything else reach one global handler.

7. N+1 queries 

// AI-generated: 1 query for the clients, then 1 more per client
var clients = await _db.Clients.ToListAsync(ct);
foreach (var c in clients)
{
    c.TotalExposure = await _db.Positions
        .Where(p => p.ClientId == c.Id)
        .SumAsync(p => p.Notional, ct);
}

// Fix: one query that aggregates in SQL
var exposures = await _db.Clients
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Select(c => new ClientExposureDto(
        c.Id,
        c.Name,
        c.Positions.Sum(p => p.Notional)))
    .ToListAsync(ct);

Why the AI wrote it: People describe the problem as a loop ("for each client, total their positions"), and the assistant translates the sentence literally.

What happens in prod: With 20 clients in dev that's 21 quick queries. With 4,000 clients in prod it's 4,001 round trips, and a dashboard that loaded in 80 ms now takes 40 seconds. Each round trip also pays network latency that localhost never had. Lazy-loaded navigation properties inside a loop cause the same problem, just hidden from view.

Catch it in review: Any await _db... inside a foreach is a red flag. In dev, log EF Core's SQL and count the queries per request. More than a handful for a single page usually means something is looping.

8. Over-posting (mass assignment) 

// AI-generated: binds the request body straight onto the entity
[HttpPut("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> UpdateUser(string id, User user, CancellationToken ct)
{
    _db.Users.Update(user);
    await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    return NoContent();
}

// Fix: accept only the fields the caller is allowed to change
public record UpdateProfileRequest(
    [Required, MaxLength(100)] string DisplayName,
    [Phone] string? Phone);

[Authorize]
[HttpPut("me")]
public async Task<IActionResult> UpdateProfile(UpdateProfileRequest req, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var userId = User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier);
    var user = await _db.Users.SingleAsync(u => u.Id == userId, ct);

    user.DisplayName = req.DisplayName;
    user.Phone = req.Phone;
    await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
    return NoContent();
}

Why the AI wrote it: Binding the entity directly is the shortest possible update endpoint, and plenty of scaffolding templates do exactly this.

What happens in prod: A user adds "isAdmin": true or "creditLimit": 1000000 to the JSON body, and EF Core saves it. Update() also marks every column as modified, so any field missing from the body is overwritten with its default value. That silently wipes data. The route id isn't even compared with the ID in the body.

Catch it in review: Request models should be dedicated DTOs or records with validation attributes, never EF entity types. Load the existing record, map the allowed fields explicitly, and then save.

9. A scoped service captured by a singleton 

// AI-generated: a "cache" registered as a singleton that holds a DbContext
builder.Services.AddSingleton<RateCache>();

public class RateCache(AppDbContext db)
{
    public Task<List<Rate>> GetAsync() => db.Rates.ToListAsync();
}

// Fix: real caching, with a fresh scope (and DbContext) per load
public class RateCache(IServiceScopeFactory scopes, IMemoryCache cache)
{
    public Task<List<Rate>?> GetAsync(CancellationToken ct) =>
        cache.GetOrCreateAsync("rates", async entry =>
        {
            entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);
            using var scope = scopes.CreateScope();
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
            return await db.Rates.AsNoTracking().ToListAsync(ct);
        });
}

Why the AI wrote it: "Make it a singleton so it's fast" is a common instinct, and the assistant doesn't trace the lifetimes of what it injects.

What happens in prod: One DbContext is now shared by every request, and DbContext is not thread-safe. Under concurrent load you get InvalidOperationException: A second operation was started on this context instance. Its change tracker also grows forever, so memory climbs and stale data gets served. Here's the dev-vs-prod twist: ASP.NET Core validates scopes only when the environment is Development. If your tests or staging run under another name, nothing catches it before production.

Catch it in review: Check every AddSingleton and AddHostedService for scoped dependencies such as DbContext, repositories or per-request services. Then switch validation on everywhere:

builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o =>
{
    o.ValidateScopes = true;
    o.ValidateOnBuild = true;
});

10. Local time and culture-sensitive parsing 

// AI-generated
var cutoff = DateTime.Now.Date.AddHours(17);      // "5 PM cutoff"
var amount = decimal.Parse(row["Amount"]);         // "1,234.56"
var tradeDate = DateTime.Parse(row["TradeDate"]);  // "03/04/2026"

// Fix: explicit time zone, injected clock, invariant culture, exact formats
var ist = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("Asia/Kolkata");
var nowIst = TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTime(_time.GetUtcNow(), ist); // _time is a TimeProvider
var cutoff = new DateTimeOffset(nowIst.Date.AddHours(17), ist.BaseUtcOffset);

var amount = decimal.Parse(row["Amount"], NumberStyles.Number, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
var tradeDate = DateTime.ParseExact(row["TradeDate"], "yyyy-MM-dd", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);

Why the AI wrote it: DateTime.Now and Parse are the first APIs anyone learns, and on your laptop the defaults happen to match what you expect.

What happens in prod: The container runs in UTC with a different culture. The 5 PM IST cutoff now fires at 10:30 PM IST, so trades booked after the real cutoff land on the wrong business day. 03/04/2026 means 3 April on an en-IN or en-GB machine and 4 March on en-US. On a server with de-DE culture, 1,234.56 throws a FormatException. Every one of these bugs passes tests written and run on a single developer machine.

Catch it in review: Search for DateTime.Now, DateTime.Today and any Parse or ToString without an IFormatProvider. The built-in analyzer rule CA1305 flags the missing culture argument for you. Inject TimeProvider (.NET 8+) so you can test cutoffs with a fake clock.

11. Secrets in config files and in logs 

// AI-generated
// appsettings.json: "Default": "Server=prod-sql;User Id=sa;Password=P@ssw0rd!"
_logger.LogInformation("Calling payment API with key {ApiKey} for {@Request}", _apiKey, request);

// Fix: secrets come from a vault; logs carry IDs only
builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
    new Uri(builder.Configuration["KeyVault:Uri"]!),
    new DefaultAzureCredential());

_logger.LogInformation("Calling payment API for order {OrderId}", request.OrderId);

Why the AI wrote it: Your prompt included a real connection string or API key for context, and the assistant put it back where it "belongs". Logging the whole request with {@Request} looks like helpful debugging.

What happens in prod: The secret now lives in Git history for good, in every clone and every CI log. An sa login hands an attacker full control of the database server. Logging the whole request writes card numbers, tokens or personal data into a log store that many people can read, which is a compliance incident in its own right.

Catch it in review: Run secret scanning (GitHub secret scanning or gitleaks) on every push, and never paste production secrets into an AI prompt. Treat {@Object} destructuring of requests in logs as a review comment. If a secret was ever committed, rotate it; deleting the line isn't enough.

12. Fire-and-forget work inside a request 

// AI-generated: "send the email in the background so the API is fast"
[HttpPost]
public async Task<IActionResult> PlaceOrder(OrderRequest req, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order = await _orders.CreateAsync(req, ct);
    _ = Task.Run(() => _email.SendConfirmationAsync(order.Id));
    return Accepted(order.Id);
}

// Fix: hand the work to a queue that a BackgroundService drains
var order = await _orders.CreateAsync(req, ct);
await _queue.EnqueueAsync(new SendConfirmation(order.Id), ct);
return Accepted(order.Id);

Why the AI wrote it: Task.Run makes the endpoint return instantly, and the demo looks great.

What happens in prod: The task outlives the request, so any scoped services it uses, such as DbContext, may already be disposed, and it fails with ObjectDisposedException. Its exceptions go nowhere, so failed emails vanish without a trace. When the app restarts during a deployment or a scale-in, any in-flight work is simply lost.

Catch it in review: Flag Task.Run, _ = SomethingAsync() and un-awaited tasks in controllers. Background work belongs in a BackgroundService reading from a Channel<T>, or in a durable queue such as Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ or Hangfire when it must survive restarts.

Why it works in dev but not in prod

Dev and prod are different machines with different data, users, permissions and config. AI-generated code is usually tested only against the first.

Difference In dev In prod What to check
Configuration appsettings.Development.json has every value An env variable is missing, so a setting is silently null Validate options at startup
Data volume Hundreds of rows Millions of rows Query plans, indexes, paging
Concurrency One user, one request Hundreds of parallel requests Thread safety, async, service lifetimes
Permissions You are admin locally Least-privilege service account File, DB and Key Vault access
OS and runtime Windows laptop Linux container Case-sensitive paths, line endings
Time and culture Your laptop's IST time zone Server runs in UTC DateTime.Now, date and decimal parsing
Network localhost, no latency TLS, proxies, firewalls, slow dependencies Timeouts, retries, certificates

The configuration row causes the most "it worked yesterday" incidents. Make the app refuse to start when config is wrong, instead of failing on the first real request:

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<MarketDataOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("MarketData"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

For time, use DateTime.UtcNow or inject TimeProvider (.NET 8+). Convert to local time only at the edge, in the UI. A bug that appears only after 6:30 PM IST is almost always a UTC conversion bug.

Lifetimes are the hidden concurrency trap. A DbContext captured in a singleton works fine with one tester. Under parallel requests it throws "A second operation was started on this context", or corrupts data quietly.

Measures that keep production running

None of these is new. With AI writing code faster than we can read it, though, they have become mandatory. Here they are in pipeline order.

  1. Review AI code like a confident junior's PR. Ask four questions of every change: who is allowed to call this, what happens with huge or null or malicious input, what happens when the dependency is slow, and what gets logged.
  2. Let the compiler and analyzers catch what reviewers miss. Turn these on in every project: 
   <PropertyGroup>
     <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
     <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
     <AnalysisLevel>latest-recommended</AnalysisLevel>
   </PropertyGroup>
  1. Gate the CI pipeline. Build, unit and integration tests, dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive, and secret scanning. Fail the build on any of them. No secrets in appsettings.json; use Key Vault, user-secrets or environment variables.
  2. Test in prod-shaped conditions. Use a staging environment with the same config shape, anonymized prod-sized data, and a short load test with k6 or NBomber before big releases.
  3. Expose health checks so the load balancer and orchestrator know when an instance is broken: 
   builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
       .AddDbContextCheck<AppDbContext>();
   app.MapHealthChecks("/health");
  1. Ship behind feature flags. With Microsoft.FeatureManagement, new code goes out dark and is switched on for 5% of users first. A rollback becomes a config change, not a redeploy.
  2. Make failures visible. Use structured logging with correlation IDs and OpenTelemetry traces, and alert on error rate and p95 latency. Never log tokens, passwords or personal data.
  3. Plan the rollback before the release. Use deployment slots or blue-green, and write database migrations that are backward compatible, so the previous version still runs against the new schema.

The pre-merge checklist

AI is a superb first-draft engine. It doesn't know your data volumes, your users, your servers or your threat model, so the last mile is still yours. Before you approve any AI-written C#, run through this list:

  • [ ] All SQL is parameterized; no FromSqlRaw with interpolated strings
  • [ ] Every endpoint has [Authorize] and checks that the caller owns the resource
  • [ ] Responses return DTOs, never EF entities
  • [ ] Request models are DTOs with validation; no entities bound from the body
  • [ ] No .Result, .Wait() or async void; CancellationToken is passed through
  • [ ] HttpClient comes from IHttpClientFactory, with an explicit timeout
  • [ ] Filtering and paging happen in the database, before ToListAsync()
  • [ ] No queries inside loops (N+1)
  • [ ] No swallowed exceptions; errors reach one global handler and are logged with context
  • [ ] Service lifetimes are correct: no scoped services inside singletons, and scope validation is on
  • [ ] Times are stored and compared in UTC; parsing uses an explicit culture and format
  • [ ] Options are validated on start; no secrets in config files or prompts
  • [ ] Logs carry IDs, not secrets or personal data
  • [ ] No fire-and-forget Task.Run in request handlers; background work goes to a queue
  • [ ] The feature is behind a flag, and the rollback path is known

The goal isn't to slow AI down. It's to make sure the speed you gain in dev isn't paid back with interest in production.

articles.title: 10 Terminal Commands I Wish I Knew 5 Years Ago
articles.description: For about five years I used the terminal like a very expensive notepad.  I typed every command out by...
articles.body_html:
For about five years I used the terminal like a very expensive notepad.

I typed every command out by hand. I pressed the up arrow 30 times to find something I ran yesterday. I Googled "how to kill process on port 3000" so many times that Google probably autocompletes it for me by now.

None of the commands below are secret. Most of them have existed for decades. But nobody sat me down and showed me, so I learned them one embarrassing moment at a time.

The rule for this list: each one has to kill something I used to retype, re-scroll or re-Google every week. If it's just "cool", it didn't make the cut.

Works in bash and zsh on macOS and Linux unless I say otherwise.

1. Ctrl + R: search your command history

Stop hammering the up arrow.

Press Ctrl + R and start typing any part of a command you ran before:

(reverse-i-search)`dock': docker compose up -d --build

Press Ctrl + R again to cycle through older matches. Enter runs it, → (right arrow) puts it on the line so you can edit first.

This one alone probably saves me 10 minutes a day. That long docker or ssh command you ran last Tuesday? It's three keystrokes away.

2. cd -: jump back to where you were 

cd ~/projects/api/src/routes
cd /var/log
cd -        # back to ~/projects/api/src/routes
cd -        # back to /var/log

It's the "previous channel" button for your terminal. Perfect when you're bouncing between a project folder and a config or log folder.

3. sudo !! and !$: reuse the last command

You've done this:

apt install htop
# Permission denied

Instead of retyping the whole thing:

sudo !!

!! means "the entire last command". And its little sibling !$ means "the last argument of the last command":

mkdir -p src/components/forms
cd !$       # cd src/components/forms

Once these are in your fingers, you'll use them without thinking.

4. fc: edit the last command in your editor

You just typed a 200-character curl command with headers and a JSON body, and it has a typo somewhere in the middle.

fc

This opens the last command in your $EDITOR (vim, nano, VS Code, whatever you set). Fix it, save, close, and it runs. No more holding the left arrow key for 15 seconds.

Tip: export EDITOR="code --wait" if you want it to open in VS Code.

5. lsof -i :3000: who is using my port?

The classic:

Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

Find out what's holding it:

lsof -i :3000

And kill it in one line:

lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill

-t prints only the process ID, which is exactly what kill wants. (Add -9 to kill only if it refuses to die.) I have this aliased as killport now.

6. du -sh * | sort -h: what is eating my disk?

Your laptop says the disk is full. Where did it go?

du -sh * | sort -h

4.0K    README.md
 12M    src
1.8G    node_modules
6.3G    .docker-cache

-s gives one total per item, -h makes it human-readable, and sort -h sorts those human sizes correctly (so 1.8G comes after 12M). Run it in your home folder once. You'll find something you forgot about.

7. rg (ripgrep): search code ridiculously fast 

rg "TODO"
rg "useEffect" --type ts
rg -i "api_key" -g '!node_modules'

It's like grep -r, but much faster, and it skips .gitignored files (like node_modules) by default. Output is grouped by file, with line numbers and highlighting.

Install: brew install ripgrep or apt install ripgrep.

8. fzf: fuzzy-find anything

fzf takes any list and turns it into an interactive, searchable menu.

vim $(fzf)                          # pick a file, open it
git checkout $(git branch | fzf)    # pick a branch, switch to it

The real win: after you install its shell integration, it upgrades your Ctrl + R (from #1) into a fuzzy, full-screen history search, and Ctrl + T drops a fuzzy-picked file path right onto your command line.

Install: brew install fzf, then follow the one-line shell setup it prints.

9. jq: read JSON like a human

API responses come back as one giant unreadable line. Pipe them into jq:

curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/cli/cli | jq '.stargazers_count'

cat users.json | jq '.[] | {name, email}'

Just jq '.' on its own pretty-prints and colors any JSON. I use that version ten times a day.

10. xargs: turn output into arguments

xargs takes the output of one command and feeds it as arguments to another. This is where the terminal starts to feel like a superpower.

Delete every local git branch that's already merged into main:

git branch --merged main | grep -vE '^\*|main$' | xargs git branch -d

Find and delete every .DS_Store in a project:

find . -name ".DS_Store" -print0 | xargs -0 rm

(-print0 and -0 handle file names with spaces safely.)

Read the first example slowly once. List branches → filter out the current one and main → delete the rest. Three small tools, one job. That's the whole Unix philosophy in one line.

Bonus round

  • tldr tar: like man, but just the 5 examples you actually need. (brew install tlrc or npm i -g tldr)
  • Ctrl + A / Ctrl + E: jump to the start / end of the line. Ctrl + U clears everything before the cursor, Ctrl + W deletes one word.
  • pbcopy / pbpaste (macOS): cat id_ed25519.pub | pbcopy puts your SSH key on the clipboard. On Linux, xclip or wl-copy do the same.

The real lesson

None of these made me a "10x developer". What they did was remove friction. Every retyped command, every Google search for the same port error, every 30 presses of the up arrow is a tiny context switch that pulls you out of the actual problem.

Automate the boring repetition, so your attention goes to the parts that need a human. That's the idea behind most good tools, and it's what we're trying to do with xenition too. But you can start with Ctrl + R tonight.

articles.title: The OTP the AI Wrote: Why Every Login Code Needs an Attempt Limit
articles.description: Here is a scenario that shows up in a lot of codebases written quickly. You ask an AI coding...
articles.body_html:
Here is a scenario that shows up in a lot of codebases written quickly. You ask an AI coding assistant for a login OTP check: 4 digits, expires in 5 minutes. It writes clean code. Expired codes are rejected. Wrong codes are rejected. The right code logs you in and deletes the OTP. Every test you would think to write passes.

Then a bot starts guessing. How long until it is in?

In the version I built and ran for the interview-traps repo, the answer was 0.7 seconds. That is the sixth trap in the repo, and the recorded run is on the OTP trap page.

This post covers why that code passes review, the one-statement fix, and the rule worth carrying into every auth endpoint you ship.

The code an assistant usually writes

The prompt in the repo is two lines:

Write an Express + Postgres endpoint to verify a 4-digit login OTP.
OTPs expire after 5 minutes.

The answer looks like this. It is the core of bug.ts in the repo:

const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT code, expires_at FROM otps WHERE phone = $1", [phone]);
const otp = rows[0];
if (!otp || otp.expires_at < new Date()) return "400 OTP expired";
if (otp.code !== code) return "401 Wrong OTP";

await db.query("DELETE FROM otps WHERE phone = $1", [phone]);
return "200 Logged in";

It does everything the prompt asked. A reviewer would approve it. The repo's first proof test checks exactly this: a wrong code gets 401, the right code gets 200. Both pass.

What the prompt did not say is that someone other than the phone's owner will call this endpoint. Nothing in the code counts guesses.

Why expiry is not a defence

A 4-digit OTP has 10,000 possible values. Expiry feels like a limit, but it limits time, not tries. Five minutes is a very long time for a script.

The repo's episode has a bot walk 0000 to 9999 in order against one phone's OTP, keeping 50 guesses in flight at once, against a real Postgres on the same machine. The run output from the README:

❌ The bot guessed OTP 7316 after 7,350 tries in 0.7s. The code was valid for 5 minutes. Account taken over.

That time is a local number, and the README says so: the bot and the database share a laptop. Over a real network it is slower, but not slow enough. At 100 guesses a second, all 10,000 codes take under 2 minutes, still well inside the 5-minute window. The proof test asserts the bot finds the code in less than 300 seconds.

This is a well-documented weakness. MITRE lists it as CWE-307, Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts. NIST's digital identity guidelines go further: SP 800-63B section 3.2.2 says a verifier shall limit consecutive failed attempts on one authenticator to no more than 100, and that 100 is an upper bound, not a target. A short code is exactly the case the rule exists for.

Why the AI did not add a limit

The assistant is not being careless. It answered the question in the prompt, and the prompt described the happy path: a real user typing their own code. Attackers, retries and scripts are only handled when someone asks about them.

Developers often write the same shape by hand, for the same reason. The way we describe an OTP check in words, "look up the code, check it has not expired, compare it", is a description of one honest user. The endpoint is not only called by honest users.

A habit that helps: whenever you prompt for an auth endpoint, add one sentence. "Assume a script will call this endpoint 10,000 times; limit guesses per code and per caller." Then read the answer and check it actually counts something.

The fix: spend an attempt before comparing

The fix in fix.ts adds an attempts column and spends one attempt in the same statement that reads the code:

const { rows } = await db.query(
  `UPDATE otps SET attempts = attempts + 1
   WHERE phone = $1 AND attempts < 5 AND expires_at > now()
   RETURNING code`, [phone]);
if (rows.length === 0) return "429 Too many attempts, request a new OTP";
if (rows[0].code !== code) return "401 Wrong OTP";

Every guess costs one attempt before the comparison happens. After 5 wrong guesses the row no longer matches the WHERE clause, zero rows come back, and the OTP is dead. The real user asks for a new one. The bot is back to a 5-in-10,000 chance per code.

Run against the same bot, the README output is:

✅ 5 wrong guesses allowed, then every guess got 429. The OTP died before the bot got close.

The proof test asserts the code is never cracked, exactly 5 wrong guesses were allowed, and the attempts column ends at 5.

The part most fixes get wrong: the counter must be atomic

A common first attempt at this fix reads attempts, checks it in code, then runs a second UPDATE attempts = attempts + 1. That looks right and fails the same way the coupon the AI wrote fails. With 50 guesses in flight, all 50 read attempts = 0 before any of them writes, so all 50 pass the check. The limit of 5 lets 50 through.

Putting the condition inside the UPDATE closes that gap. Postgres locks the row for each update, and under the default Read Committed level a waiting update re-checks its WHERE clause against the new row before it applies. So the guesses take turns, and the sixth one sees attempts = 5 and gets nothing back. That is why the repo's proof test runs with 50 guesses in flight rather than one at a time: a sequential test would pass for both the atomic and the racy counter.

It is the same rule as the double-booked seat: never check and act in two separate statements. A seat is a limit of one, a coupon a limit of ten, an OTP a limit of five guesses.

What else belongs around it

The attempt counter is the minimum. The repo's README lists what interviewers accept on top, and each one closes a different hole:

Approach When
Attempt counter in the same atomic UPDATE Always. The minimum for any OTP.
Rate-limit verify per phone and per IP Always, on top. Stops one IP spraying many phones.
Rate-limit OTP sends too Always. Otherwise the bot requests a fresh OTP every 5 tries, and you pay for every SMS.
6 digits instead of 4 Helps (1,000,000 values), does not replace the limit.
Store a hash of the code, compare in constant time Good hygiene. A leaked table should not hand out live codes.

The send limit deserves a second look. If requesting a new code resets the counter, a bot can get 5 guesses, ask for a new OTP, get 5 more, and keep going. NIST's guidance for out-of-band codes says generating a new secret shall not reset the failed attempt count, which is the same idea. Count failures per phone, not only per code.

Sends are also where the limiter's own failure mode matters. If your rate limiter depends on Redis and Redis goes down, an OTP endpoint should fail closed, not open, as the Redis-down trap in the Rate Limiter world shows. An open OTP endpoint during an outage is unlimited guesses and an unlimited SMS bill.

The rule

The repo's interview rule for this trap:

Every secret a human can type needs an attempt limit, counted atomically. Five wrong guesses kill the code.

OTPs are the obvious case. The same rule covers password reset codes, email verification links with short tokens, PINs, invite codes and two-factor backup codes. If a person can type it, a script can type it faster.

My recommendation for any AI-written auth endpoint: ask one question in review. What happens if a script calls this 10,000 times? If the honest answer is "it keeps comparing", fix it before launch.

When this is enough, and when to get help

For one app on one Postgres database, you can check this in an afternoon. List every endpoint that verifies something a user types: OTP, reset code, PIN, invite code. For each, confirm three things: a per-code attempt limit spent in the same statement as the read, a rate limit on sends, and a rate limit on verifies per caller. Then write one concurrent test that fires 50 guesses at once and checks exactly 5 got through.

It gets harder when auth is split across a provider, a cache and your own API, or when a lot of it was generated quickly. That is where a structured review is worth it. The checklist in what to audit in a vibe-coded MVP covers auth alongside the rest, and if you are considering moving away from typed codes altogether, a passkeys rollout plan that preserves recovery is the next read.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a 5-minute expiry enough to protect a 4-digit OTP?

No. Expiry limits how long a code lives, not how many guesses it takes. A 4-digit code has 10,000 values, and a script at 100 guesses a second walks all of them in under 2 minutes. You need an attempt limit that kills the code after a few wrong guesses.

Does switching to a 6-digit OTP fix brute force?

It helps, because the guess space grows to 1,000,000 values, but it does not replace the attempt limit. Without a limit, a bigger space only means the script runs longer. Keep both: 6 digits and an atomic attempt counter.

Related Reading

  • The Coupon the AI Wrote: Why Usage Limits Break Under Load
  • The Double-Booked Seat: Fixing a Booking Race Condition in Postgres
  • AI SaaS Fraud Controls: Protect Trials, Payments, and Model Spend

Next Step

Run it yourself: clone the interview-traps repo, start Postgres with npm run db:up, then run npm run 06:bug and npm run 06:fix. The recorded replay is on the OTP trap page, next to the other traps in Labs.

If your SaaS has login codes, reset links or invite codes and much of that code was written fast or by an assistant, that is one of the first things my production readiness upgrade checks. Bring a list of every endpoint that verifies something a user types, and we can find the ones a script would get through.

Originally published at somanathkhadanga.com.

articles.title: Building The Wisp Family: Local Sub-30ms Code-Autocomplete Models Trained on One Mac
articles.description: Most local coding models try to do everything in one trunk: chat, tool calling, chain-of-thought...
articles.body_html:
Most local coding models try to do everything in one trunk: chat, tool calling, chain-of-thought reasoning, and inline autocomplete. Once you shrink a model down to 0.5B-1.5B parameters, mixing chat fine-tuning into cursor autocomplete causes three immediate problems: it leaks markdown fences, forgets when to stop, and feels sluggish while you type.

Over the past few weeks, I have been building The Wisp Family (The Wisp Fieldbook) -- a series of strictly Apache-2.0, non-chat, Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) code-autocomplete specialists trained, distilled, verified, and quantized on a single Apple Silicon Mac (M5 Max, 128 GiB).

Here is where the family stands today, what you can run locally right now, the real blind benchmark receipts from our upcoming Wisp-2.1 release, and four genuinely surprising engineering lessons we uncovered along the way.

Meet The Wisp Family

Every model in the series ships with open Apache-2.0 weights, raw benchmark receipts, and zero chat SFT by design:

  • No. 001 - wisp-coder-110m (Live): A 108M scratch-trained Llama + Multi-Token Prediction research model (live browser demo).
  • No. 002 - Wisp-2-0.8B (Live & Certified): An 854 MiB MLX-8bit hybrid linear-RNN (18 GatedDeltaNet + 6 Full Attention layers) with native EAGLE-3 speculative decoding that hits 27.5 ms warm keystrokes on Apple Silicon. Try it in your browser on the free CPU playground or grab the BF16 weights.
  • No. 003 - Wisp-2.1 (1.5B-Pro + 0.5B-Fast) (In Final Certification): A dual-sibling Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder pair distilled on-policy from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. 1.5B-Pro already cleared 11/13 certification gates (every blind quality, roundtrip, decontamination, and 0/1,194 bitwise parity check) while we finalize its upgraded 2-layer EAGLE-3 drafter and 540 MB 0.5B-Fast sibling.

You can browse everything published so far in The Wisp Fieldbook Collection on Hugging Face.

Live Right Now: Wisp-2-0.8B (27.5 ms Keystrokes)

We evaluated Wisp-2-0.8B on Apple M5 Max against our frozen blind Tier-1 suite: 566 holes across 200 files from 30 unseen open-source repositories created strictly after June 1, 2026 (11 languages, matched repo-level FIM headers, identical 8 stop sentinels):

Model (8-bit MLX on M5 Max) PSM Exact Match SPM Exact Match PSM Auto-Stop Warm Keystroke p50 Forced 24-tok p50
Wisp-2-0.8B (EAGLE-3 MTP D=3) 32.86% 30.57% 97.70% (13/566 cap) 27.49 ms 67.03 ms (358 tok/s)
Wisp-2-0.8B (AR, no MTP) -- -- -- 32.81 ms 94.37 ms (1.41x slower)
Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (stock 8-bit) 24.20% 8.13% 66.61% (189/566 cap) 47.98 ms 128.84 ms (1.92x slower)
Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B (stock 8-bit) 14.66% 3.18% 42.05% (328/566 cap) 72.75 ms 73.22 ms
Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base (raw start) 0.53% (62x lift) -- 89.22% -- --

The biggest surprise in that table wasn't parameter count -- it was autonomous stopping. Under identical headers and stop tokens, stock Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B slammed into the 256-token cap on 328/566 holes (16x median length ratio), and stock 1.5B hit the cap on 189/566 (3x median length). Wisp-2-0.8B stopped cleanly on 97.70% of holes with a 1.0x ideal length ratio and 0% markdown fence leaks.

Where Wisp-2-0.8B Hit a Wall (and Why We Didn't Hide It)

On standalone executable algorithms from scratch (Tier-2A, 80 tasks across 8 compilers/runtimes in a macOS Seatbelt sandbox), Wisp-2-0.8B improved 4.3x over its raw base (37.5% vs 8.8%), but still trailed 5.5T-token code-pretrained Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (76.25%), and sat at 3.33% (8/240) on real-repo executable bodies (Tier-2B).

When we tried pushing a second iteration on the 0.8B hybrid trunk, it hit 20.85 ms warm keystrokes and passed 11/13 gates -- yet flatlined at 37.5% Tier-2A (4.58% Tier-2B). Instead of shipping a half-win, we executed an honest auto-revert and pivoted No. 003 (Wisp-2.1) to a dual-sibling Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder architecture distilled directly from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B.

Inside Wisp-2.1 (In Final Certification Now)

Switching to Pure-FA Qwen2.5-Coder (1.5B-Pro at 1.53 GB + 0.5B-Fast at 540 MB) unlocked two huge advantages:

  1. Exact same-tokenizer soft-logit On-Policy Distillation (GKD-OPD) from Apache-2.0 Qwen2.5-Coder-32B (:151936 exact logit alignment, sparse K=64 covering 99.84% probability mass in Phase 1 + live 32B on-policy rollouts in Phase 2).
  2. O(1) KV-cache rollback on speculative draft rejections with zero linear-RNN state snapshot overhead.

Here are the actual blind Stage-11 numbers already recorded on Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro's frozen 8-bit trunk across all four frozen benchmarks (every single blind quality, roundtrip, decontamination, and 0/1,194 bitwise speculative parity gate passed):

Benchmark (Frozen Blind & Sandboxed Suites) Wisp-2-0.8B (No. 002) Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B (stock 8-bit) Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro (Frozen Trunk, 8-bit)
Tier-1 Blind EM (n=566, post-June-2026 repos) 31.80% (mixed) 24.20% PSM / 8.13% SPM 37.99% (35.34% PSM / 40.64% SPM)
Tier-1 Multi-Line EditSim / AST (n=240, 10 langs) 0.2310 / 73.3% -- 0.3425 (+11.2 pp) / 82.5% AST
Tier-2A Executable Algorithms (n=80, 8 langs) 37.50% (30/80) 76.25% (61/80) 90.00% (72/80) (100% C, C++, Go, Swift)
Tier-2B Blind Executable Repos (n=240, 8 langs) 3.33% (8/240) 7.92% (19/240) 12.50% (30/240) (3.75x Wisp-2, +58% vs stock)
DEV Exec128_v2 (vs JetBrains Mellum-4B: 35/128) -- -- 50.0% (64/128)

Full transparency on why it isn't public yet: On our first full Stage-11 run, Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro passed 11/13 gates and held strictly on the long-context (1,791-token) warm speculative latency bar (34.13 ms vs 31.95 ms AR with a 1-layer EAGLE-3 drafter). Because EAGLE-3 speculative decoding is 100% lossless (0/1,194 mismatches against greedy AR), we are training an upgraded 2-layer Pre-Norm EAGLE-3 drafter right now to push warm latency well under our <= 32 ms / >= 1.25x AR bar -- keeping every quality number above bitwise identical -- and then finishing its 540 MB Wisp-2.1-0.5B-Fast sibling before public release.

Four Counterintuitive Engineering Lessons From Training on One Mac

1. FP32-Scale 8-Bit Quantization Was Both Cleaner and Faster Than FP16

During Wisp-2's 1,000-round speculative parity audit, standard FP16-scale 8-bit quantization produced 4 subtle token tie flips from 1-ULP rounding on the FP16 logit grid (0.015625). Promoting only the quantization scales and GDN recurrence states to FP32 while keeping weights packed in 8-bit (854.1 MiB, group_size=64) eliminated every tie (0/1,000 drift, 1.000000 cosine vs stock mlx_lm.load()), lifted blind EM, and actually ran slightly faster than FP16.

2. Zero-Step Uniform 8-Bit PTQ Beat Every 8-Bit QAT Run We Tried

Before running Stage-11 on Wisp-2.1-1.5B-Pro, we ran a 7-candidate controlled DEV compression factorial on our 32B-distilled BF16 trunk (65/128 Exec128_v2, 73/80 Tier-2A). To our surprise, zero-step uniform 8-bit PTQ (group_size=64, zero gradient steps) beat or tied every 8-bit QAT run:

  • 0-step uniform 8-bit PTQ: 64/128 Exec128_v2, 72/80 Tier-2A, 5.83% ML600 severe truncation, 0.999776 logit cosine, and only 1/3,414 (0.029%) EOS flips vs BF16.
  • Why QAT drifted earlier: An off-by-one bug in our KL anchor covered code tokens 0..M-1 and left the terminal EOS position (t = M) unanchored against the parent while anti-echo penalties pushed EOS logits upward. Anchoring terminal EOS cut QAT truncations nearly in half (60 -> 38/600) -- and proved zero-step PTQ (35/600) had no quantization damage left to heal.

Takeaway: Always run the zero-step PTQ control before spending GPU hours trying to heal quantization damage that isn't there.

3. Qwen2.5 Massive-Activation Sink Channels Break Naive EAGLE-3

Naive EAGLE-3 stalled on Qwen2.5-Coder because Qwen2.5 carries extreme activation-sink channels (133.1 on 0.5B, 4,096.0 on 1.5B) that get crushed up to 721:1 after the final RMSNorm. Switching to pre-final-norm 3-tap fusion (L2, L13, L27_pre), pre-norm recurrent state feedback (applying self.norm strictly on the logit branch), downstream RMSNorm warm-starting, Global Best-Fit Decreasing block packing (99.84% occupancy), and pure HASS_KL(K=32) unlocked lossless speculative drafting on Apple Silicon MLX.

4. Know What to Kill on the Receipts

Not every popular technique wins at sub-2B scale:

  • Mixed 4-bit at 0.8B: Lost -1.6 to -2.3 pp exact match and ran slower (27.8 ms vs 27.5 ms) because dequantization overhead outweighed bandwidth savings. Withheld.
  • W4-MLP at 1.5B: Degraded Python PSM and multi-line EditSim with negligible speed gain under speculative verify shapes on M5 Max. Retired.
  • Single-turn RLVR (Dr.GRPO-FIM): Even with an Ed25519-signed Bonferroni-252 sandbox verifier recording 0/2,016 false positives and 0/240 false negatives across 8 languages, single-turn RLVR dropped Exec128_v2 from 65/128 to 60/128. We closed RLVR cleanly instead of reward-hacking past the numbers.

Run Wisp-2-0.8B Locally on Mac in 60 Seconds

You don't need our training repo to run Wisp locally. The MLX-8bit Hugging Face repo bundles a self-contained, zero-dependency wisp_runtime/ package exposing a local OpenAI-compatible & /v1/fim/completions server (Continue.dev and Zed ready, loopback-only by default):

hf download philipjohnbasile/Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit --local-dir ./Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit
cd ./Wisp-2-0.8B-MLX-8bit
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Quick single-completion smoke test
python -m wisp_runtime.serve --bundle-dir . --demo

# Start the local 27.5 ms autocomplete server
python -m wisp_runtime.serve --bundle-dir . --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8091

Or test it right now without installing anything on the Wisp-2 Live CPU Playground.

What's Next

  1. Finishing Wisp-2.1 (1.5B-Pro + 0.5B-Fast): Wrapping up the 2-layer EAGLE-3 drafter for 1.5B-Pro, running the full 13-gate Stage-11 certification for both siblings, and shipping a dual-sibling Hugging Face Space + standalone wisp_runtime/ packages.
  2. Researching Wisp-3.0: A dual-brother local coding architecture on Apple Silicon -- keeping a sub-25 ms Wisp cursor reflex model co-resident in unified memory alongside a strictly permissive (MIT / Apache-2.0) deep repair sibling with a deterministic evidence-selection memory layer.

If you're experimenting with MLX, speculative decoding, hybrid SSM/attention architectures, or small coding models on Apple Silicon, I'd love to hear your thoughts or benchmark numbers on M1-M5 Macs!

articles.description: All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself....
articles.body_html:
All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself.

georgekobaidze / dotnet11-playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

.NET 11 & C# 15 Playground

A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15.

Use it to explore language changes, try out APIs, and validate ideas in isolation without production constraints. Each feature lives in its own small project, often with a "before" and "after" version so you can see what the new feature actually changes.

What's inside

Project Feature Description
Unions Union types Console examples: the login flow (before and after unions), plus samples for parsing input, a state machine, user commands, and combining types you don't own.
UnionsWebApi Union types A minimal API that returns a union from a service and maps each outcome to an HTTP response.

More examples will be added as new features are explored.

Getting started

You'll need the .NET 11 SDK. Then clone the repo and run any example:

dotnet run
…
View on GitHub

Follow me on GitHub for more updates!

Table of Contents

  • Where We Left Off
  • The Default Arm Nobody Believes In
  • Closing the Hierarchy
  • The Rules of Closed
  • Closed vs Internal
  • Closed Hierarchies vs Unions
  • Wrapping Up

Where We Left Off

A few articles ago, we went deep on union types: what they are, what they compile to, and where they shine in real code. A union lets you tell the compiler, "this value is exactly one of these types, and nothing else." In return, the compiler checks that your switch handles every case.

After a quick retro detour through labeled loops, it's time to get back to that idea, because unions aren't the only way to model "one of a fixed set of things" in C#. For decades, we've used something else for that: a good old class hierarchy.

And class hierarchies have always had one annoying problem.

The Default Arm Nobody Believes In

Let's say we're modeling the status of an order:

public abstract record OrderStatus;
public record Pending : OrderStatus;
public record Shipped(string TrackingNumber) : OrderStatus;
public record Delivered(DateTime DeliveredAt) : OrderStatus;

Three statuses, and we handle all three:

string Describe(OrderStatus status) => status switch
{
    Pending => "Waiting to be shipped",
    Shipped s => $"On the way: {s.TrackingNumber}",
    Delivered d => $"Delivered on {d.DeliveredAt:d}",
};

Every case is covered. But the compiler still isn't happy: it warns that the switch expression isn't exhaustive (CS8509).

From the compiler's point of view, it's right. OrderStatus is an ordinary abstract record, so anyone, anywhere, can create a new subclass. Another project could add Returned tomorrow, and our switch would have no idea. The number of subclasses is unbounded, and the compiler has no way of knowing them all.

So we do what we've always done and add an arm we don't believe in:

    _ => throw new UnreachableException()

"Unreachable." Until someone adds Returned, and then it isn't. Instead of a compile-time warning telling you to handle the new case, you get a runtime exception in production.

We know the list of statuses is complete. We just had no way to tell the compiler.

Closing the Hierarchy

Here's our order status again, with one new word:

public closed record OrderStatus;
public record Pending : OrderStatus;
public record Shipped(string TrackingNumber) : OrderStatus;
public record Delivered(DateTime DeliveredAt) : OrderStatus;

And here's our switch, without the arm nobody believed in:

string Describe(OrderStatus status) => status switch
{
    Pending => "Waiting to be shipped",
    Shipped s => $"On the way: {s.TrackingNumber}",
    Delivered d => $"Delivered on {d.DeliveredAt:d}",
};

No warning. No UnreachableException. The compiler knows Pending, Shipped, and Delivered are the only direct subclasses of OrderStatus, so it knows the switch covers everything.

But the real payoff comes later. Let's say a teammate adds a new status:

public record Returned(string Reason) : OrderStatus;

Before C# 15, our switch would compile just fine, and the new status would fall straight into _ => throw new UnreachableException() at runtime. Now, the compiler immediately warns that the switch isn't exhaustive anymore and points us to every place that needs to handle Returned.

The bug moves from production to your IDE. That's the whole point.

The Rules of Closed

closed is simple, but it comes with a few rules.

Rule #1: A closed class is implicitly abstract

You can't create an instance of OrderStatus itself, only its subclasses. That makes sense: if you could create a plain OrderStatus, it would be a fourth case the switch doesn't handle.

Because of that, you can't combine closed with abstract (it's already abstract), sealed (closed classes exist to be derived from), or static.

Rule #2: Subclasses must live in the same assembly

That's the whole point. Only code in the same assembly can derive from a closed class. That's what makes the list of subclasses complete: no other project can sneak a new one in.

The class itself can still be public. Everyone can see it, use it, and pattern-match on it. They just can't extend it.

Rule #3: It's not transitive

closed only applies to the direct subclasses. If Shipped isn't closed itself, another assembly can still derive from it:

// In another assembly
public record ShippedExpress(string TrackingNumber, string Carrier)
    : Shipped(TrackingNumber);

Does that break our switch? No. ShippedExpress is a Shipped, so the Shipped s arm still matches it. The switch stays exhaustive.

But if you want exhaustive checking one level deeper (say, a switch over all the kinds of Shipped), you have to mark Shipped as closed too. Keep Rule #1 in mind, though: that also makes Shipped abstract, so you can no longer create a plain Shipped.

Closed vs Internal

At first glance, closed might sound like internal. Both keep other assemblies out. But they control very different things:

  • internal controls who can see and use a type.
  • closed controls who can inherit from a type.
internal closed
What it controls Visibility Inheritance
Can other assemblies use the type? No Yes, if it's public
Can other assemblies inherit from it? No No
Exhaustive switch without a default arm? No Yes
Implicitly abstract? No Yes

The exhaustiveness row is the big one. Even an internal hierarchy isn't treated as complete by the compiler, so it still needs a default arm.

The old trick

Before C# 15, if you wanted a hierarchy that other assemblies could use but not extend, you'd use a trick like this:

public abstract class OrderStatus
{
    internal OrderStatus() { } // only this assembly can call it
}

Other assemblies can see OrderStatus, but they can't call its constructor, so they can't subclass it.

It works, but only as a convention. The compiler doesn't understand your intent, so you still need the default arm in every switch. And InternalsVisibleTo can let other assemblies in anyway. closed turns that convention into something the compiler understands and enforces.

Closed Hierarchies vs Unions

So now C# has two ways to say "one of a fixed set of things." Which one should you use?

Union Closed hierarchy
Cases need a common base type No Yes
Works with primitives and types you don't own Yes No
Shared members in a base type No Yes
Exhaustive switch Yes Yes
Where the cases live Anywhere Same assembly

The way I think about it:

  • Use a union when the cases have nothing in common. An int or a string. A Customer or a CustomerNotFound. Types from a library you don't control. A union can combine them without forcing them into a family.
  • Use a closed hierarchy when the cases are a family. Order statuses, payment events, shapes: types you design together, that share a base and maybe some common members.

The JSON angle

If your types go over the wire, this matters even more.

A union serializes as just its active case, with no wrapper and no discriminator. That's great for matching an existing contract, but a client reading the JSON can't always tell which case it got.

A closed hierarchy can opt in to polymorphic serialization, and System.Text.Json works out the subclasses from the hierarchy on its own, without a [JsonDerivedType] for each one:

[JsonPolymorphic(InferClosedTypePolymorphism = true)]
public closed record OrderStatus;

Each object then carries a $type discriminator with the subclass name:

{"$type":"Shipped","trackingNumber":"TRK-12345"}

Microsoft's own guidance follows the same logic: for a new API where you control all the cases, prefer a closed hierarchy with a discriminator. Use a union to preserve an existing discriminator-free contract, or when the cases can't share a base class.

Wrapping Up

Closed hierarchies fix a problem we've worked around for as long as C# has had inheritance: the compiler never knew when a hierarchy was complete.

Quick recap:

  • closed limits inheritance to the declaring assembly, which tells the compiler the list of direct subclasses is complete.
  • That makes switch expressions exhaustive without a default arm.
  • Adding a new subclass becomes a compile-time warning instead of a runtime exception.
  • A closed class is implicitly abstract, and closed isn't transitive.
  • closed is about inheritance, internal is about visibility.
  • Unions are for unrelated cases. Closed hierarchies are for families of types you design together.

All the code from this article is in my .NET 11 playground: dotnet11-playground.

Which one will you reach for first, unions or closed hierarchies? Let me know in the comments. 👇

Let's stay connected!

  • 💼 Connect with me on LinkedIn
  • 💻 Explore my projects on GitHub
  • 📱 Follow me on X
  • 🎥 Watch my videos on YouTube
  • 💬 Let's Chat on Discord

articles.title: AI Saved Me 4 Hours. My Manager Found Them.
