articles.body_html:
AI was supposed to save us time.

Somehow, my deadlines got shorter instead. 🙃

As a developer, I absolutely love what AI enables me to do today. Experimenting with ideas, building prototypes, exploring new technologies and implementing features has never been easier.

That random side project I thought about six months ago? I can probably build an MVP this weekend.

But there's something strange happening.

We're coding faster. We're shipping more. We're constantly busy.

Yet, somehow, we have less time.

🚀 Yesterday's Superpower Is Today's Expectation

Remember when implementing a feature in a week was perfectly reasonable?

Now the conversation goes something like this:

Manager: How long will this take?

Developer: Probably two days.

Manager: But you have AI, right?

Developer: 💀

A week's work becomes a day's work. A few hours of work becomes a few minutes of work.

Every productivity improvement seems to come with an automatic deadline reduction.

AI saves me four hours, and somehow my backlog gets four hours bigger.

It's like upgrading your internet connection only to have everyone send you larger files.

🧠 Introducing Context Debt

We all know technical debt. But I think we're accumulating another kind of debt.

Context Debt.

Previously, writing code was also a process of understanding the system. We explored the codebase, understood dependencies, discovered edge cases and questioned architectural decisions.

Today, our workflow sometimes looks like this:

Prompt → Generate → Accept → Test → Commit → Repeat

Everything works.

Until it doesn't.

Suddenly, you're staring at a function you technically wrote but have absolutely no recollection of writing.

Git blame says it's you.

Your brain strongly disagrees.

That's context debt — the gap between how much our codebase grows and how much we actually understand it.

  • Technical debt makes code harder to maintain.
  • Context debt makes code harder to understand, debug and confidently change.

And unlike technical debt, your linter probably won't warn you about it.

🏃 The Illusion of Moving Faster

Here's a fictional but painfully relatable example.

Task Without AI With AI
Understanding the problem 30 min 5 min
Writing code 90 min 5 min
Testing 30 min 30 min
Debugging 30 min 120 min
Understanding what went wrong — 40 min
Total 180 min 200 min

Illustrative numbers, not a benchmark.

The feature was implemented in five minutes!

Let's celebrate. 🎉

Never mind the three hours we spent making it actually work.

We often measure how quickly we generate the first implementation rather than how quickly we deliver a reliable solution.

More commits. More pull requests. More closed tickets.

It certainly looks like progress.

But your GitHub contribution graph isn't necessarily a productivity graph.

Activity !== Progress

🐛 AI vs. Debugging

My favourite AI debugging workflow:

Me: Fix this bug.

AI: I've identified the root cause.

Me: It still doesn't work.

AI: You're absolutely right.
    I've now identified the actual root cause.

Me: That's a different bug.

AI: Great catch!

Three prompts later, I've modified seven files to fix a two-line issue.

Sound familiar?

AI is genuinely useful for debugging. But when we don't understand the original implementation, it becomes harder to evaluate whether the suggested fix actually makes sense.

We slowly transition from:

"Why is this happening?"

to:

"Please make it stop happening."

One builds understanding. The other might just make the error disappear.

🔥 Production Has Entered the Chat

Everything works on localhost.

All tests pass.

The AI confidently tells you the implementation is robust and production-ready.

Production: Hold my beer. 🍺

Real-world systems have distributed services, race conditions, stale caches, infrastructure issues, unexpected traffic patterns and undocumented business logic.

Production incidents don't come with perfectly structured prompts.

They come with incomplete logs, intermittent failures and a Slack channel full of people asking for an ETA.

AI can help analyse the symptoms, but understanding the system is still critical.

Why was that workaround introduced six months ago? Why does this service behave differently under load? Why is that seemingly unnecessary condition actually necessary?

If we've lost that context, even AI-assisted debugging becomes harder.

You can generate a microservice in minutes. Understanding why it's failing in production at 2 AM is a different story.

🔄 The AI Productivity Trap

Here's the cycle I worry about:

AI makes coding faster
        ↓
Expectations increase
        ↓
Deadlines get shorter
        ↓
Less time to understand
        ↓
Context debt increases
        ↓
Debugging becomes harder
        ↓
More dependency on AI
        ↓
     Repeat 🔁

Interestingly, the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey found that 66% of respondents cited AI solutions that were almost right as a frustration, while 45% cited time-consuming debugging of AI-generated code.

It doesn't mean AI makes everyone slower.

But perhaps some of the time we're saving on implementation is being spent elsewhere.

☕ Can We Have Some of That Time Back?

I'm not anti-AI. Quite the opposite.

I love experimenting with AI. It makes software development exciting in ways that weren't possible before.

But wouldn't it be nice if some of the time saved went towards:

  • Understanding our codebases better.
  • Fixing that technical debt everyone keeps ignoring.
  • Improving architecture and observability.
  • Learning something new.
  • Experimenting without a deadline.
  • Actually finishing our coffee while it's hot.

Not every hour saved needs to become another hour of work.

The Real Irony

We are writing more code but potentially understanding less of it.

We are implementing features faster, but not necessarily resolving problems faster.

We have better tools, but increasingly unrealistic deadlines.

Perhaps the next challenge in the AI era isn't making AI faster.

It's figuring out what to do with the speed we already have.

AI should make our lives easier, not just our sprint backlogs bigger.

I'm curious about your experience.

  • Has AI actually given you more time, or has it just increased what everyone expects from you?
  • Are you coding faster but debugging longer?
  • Do you still understand the code that Git blame says you wrote? 😄

Let's discuss in the comments.

AI disclosure: The observations and perspectives are my own, with AI assistance in drafting and editorial refinement.

articles.title: I Built a Memory That Learns From Failure. Then I Couldn't Find a Failure to Feed It.
articles.description: A few weeks ago I wrote a post here arguing that my cheap models weren't dumb, they were missing a...
articles.body_html:
A few weeks ago I wrote a post here arguing that my cheap models weren't dumb, they were missing a world model. It was 90% hypothesis and 10% hope. I had read about a third of a paper and built nothing.

This is the report from actually building it.

It does not end with a benchmark. It ends with two memory systems, one week of work I walked out of early, and a measurement problem I didn't see coming.

The setup, quickly

I build Mocu, an open-source, local-first desktop AI colleague. You bring your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which means I spend most of my time running it on cheap models, because that's the whole point of the thing.

And cheap models repeat themselves.

They try the same failing command twice. They read a wrong path, notice the path was wrong, and then read the wrong path again five minutes later with total confidence. Every tool I used before this explained the mistake to me beautifully, in detail, afterwards. Thanks. I already knew it broke.

What I wanted was the opposite: tell the model no, don't do that before the command runs. Not a post-mortem. A prediction.

The paper that gave me a shape for this is Self-Evolving World Models for LLM Agent Planning (EMNLP 2026 Findings). The short version: keep the agent frozen, and let a world model improve by evolving its context instead of its weights. Episodic memory of real action→outcome transitions, semantic memory that turns a bad prediction into a written rule, and a confidence filter that drops predictions the system doesn't believe.

No gradients. No training run. The improvement lives in text files.

That last part is why it fit my constraints at all. Mocu is Apache 2.0 and everything lives in local files you can read and edit. There's no server collecting traces and no pipeline to rent. Text is the only kind of learning I can actually ship.

Day one and two: I built a pipe

Day one went into finishing the paper. No code.

Day two I built exactly one thing: I routed every tool call the agent makes through the world-model code. Now the system physically sits between the agent and its tools. The agent cannot act without passing through it.

That felt great for about ten minutes.

Then I realized I had built a pipe and had no idea what was supposed to flow through it. How does a prediction get made? How does the agent even understand one when it arrives? Is it a warning, a rewritten plan, a blocked call? I had no answer, and the paper didn't hand me one I could wire into a real running system.

So I did what I usually do: left the question open and built the part I could build.

Day three: the "simple" one

Episodic memory. Store what the agent did, read it back, warn before it repeats a failure. In the paper this is half a page. It looked trivial.

It took a full day and forced me to reverse two things I felt strongly about.

One: where the data lives. Mocu already keeps every tool call in the project folder. My instinct was not to duplicate it. I tested that and it didn't hold. It had to go into the global folder as well.

Two: how much to store. I did not want to write every single tool call into a memory database. It felt wasteful and messy.

I now write every single tool call into it.

Both decisions came out against my instinct and I'm still not sure either one is final. "Simple" should come with a health warning.

The mechanism, plainly:

  1. Every tool call gets stored with its outcome.
  2. Before an action, a BM25 search pulls the closest past calls, and a small decision model picks the one that's genuinely closest.
  3. The system checks how that past call turned out.
  4. If it worked: silence, nothing happens.
  5. If it failed: the model gets one line. This is very close to something that failed before.

Before, not after. That's the entire feature.

And then it worked better than I expected. Noticeably better. Fewer repeated mistakes, in early tests the difference wasn't subtle.

Which should have been the happy ending, and instead gave me a small alarm. Everything I know about this project says the real world ruins your nice plan. Here, the piece I thought would eat half a day behaved better than the paper promised and better than I designed it to. So something underneath might be wrong and just hasn't shown up yet.

I went into the next day more worried than I was before the win.

Day four: the tired one

Semantic memory is the part that was supposed to do the actual thinking.

The theory: a tool fails. First question, was it that tool's fault? A bad command, a wrong path, a malformed argument? Then it belongs to episodic memory and it's already handled. If not, the real cause is further back. So you walk backwards through the earlier calls, find the tool that actually caused the failure, and turn that into a warning so the agent doesn't repeat it.

The tool that fails is often not the tool that caused it. That's the whole reason this layer needs to exist.

That was the plan. It is not what I built.

I started that day exhausted. The hardest piece of the system, and I was running on empty. So I did the thing this project keeps making possible and probably shouldn't: I let Mocu write a large part of it.

The code runs. It exists. I don't trust it, because I didn't write most of it and I haven't reviewed it properly. My honest note to myself that evening was one sentence: I don't think it turned out well.

It also diverged from the paper. The paper's version is about cause and effect, actual reasoning about how one step produced the next outcome. That didn't make it in. What made it in is a much lighter mechanism that borrowed the name and very little else.

The paper called it semantic memory. So I call it semantic memory. The name stuck. The idea didn't.

Then the test, and the joke

I built the two memories in the wrong order, and that turned out to be a trap.

In the entire test session, there was exactly one failure that the second system could legitimately catch and fix.

One.

Everything else was either already caught by episodic memory or wasn't in semantic memory's category at all. The first memory guarded the door so well that the second one never got a customer.

No bug to fix. No proof of success either. Not broken, not proven. Just unmeasured.

Why I stopped at one week

I could keep going. I could write scenarios designed specifically to feed the second memory.

But the entire premise is that it learns from real mistakes, from real work, not incidents I invented to make my own test look good. Which means the honest test isn't a test. It's weeks of using Mocu normally, waiting for enough real failures to pile up that the system has something to study.

Weeks, not days. And I don't have weeks for this right now.

So the build is finished. Not because it's proven, but because it's finished. I'm walking away and letting reality do the testing. That's how it ended: one week out of the two I gave myself, two memories, one visibly working, one I can't see yet.

The actual lesson, which isn't about memory

I spent a week building something whose entire job is to prevent mistakes, and found out that prevention is a terrible thing to measure.

Every mistake it stops is a mistake that never appears in your logs. So you end up trusting a system based on the absence of evidence, which is the exact thing you're told never to do.

Three times in this project reality argued with my plan. I thought the architecture would be easy and the magic would be hard. It was backwards. I thought the simple memory would take half a day. It took the whole day. I thought a working memory would prove itself. It didn't. It just made the second one invisible.

Maybe that's the real shape of self-improving systems. Not a moment where it gets smart. Just a slow pile of mistakes that stop happening.

What's next, and what I want to know

Two failure modes are on my short list and both are embarrassing:

  • Self-confirming memory. If the agent retrieves its own past predictions instead of past outcomes, it will happily agree with itself forever. The store has to be outcomes only.
  • Rules that breed superstition. Enough one-off heuristics and your context window becomes a collection of coincidences. Requiring a pattern to recur before promoting it is probably the fix, and it means the system learns slower, maybe not at all in a session.

If you've built something in this direction (externalized prediction, memory that writes its own rules, agents that are allowed to say "no idea"), I'd like to hear what broke. Especially the part where the memory poisoned itself.

And if you think the whole premise is wrong, that's useful too. Tell me which of those two gets me first.

I'll come back with numbers either way, including the ones that make me look bad. Mocu is open source at github.com/kharchangai/Mocu if you want to read the code before I've reviewed it.

articles.title: NodFirst: make your AI coding agent wait for your yes
articles.description: Ask a coding agent to "build me an app" and it will start building. Along the way it decides what...
articles.body_html:
Ask a coding agent to "build me an app" and it will start building. Along the way it decides what your words meant, which edge cases matter and which libraries to add. You often find out after the code exists.

NodFirst is my attempt to move those decisions in front of the code. It is a Spec-Driven Development kit for AI coding agents, written in plain Markdown. Its rule is simple: nothing gets built until you say yes.

How it works

A request becomes a short series of documents, each one a file in your repository:

init / adopt → specify → (clarify) → (design) → plan → tasks → analyze → implement → verify

The spec says what you want, the plan says how, and the tasks cut it into small steps. After each phase the agent stops and waits for your approval, which is recorded in the file.

Three rules do most of the work:

  • No silent decisions. When your words can be read two ways, the agent asks or lists the reading it chose.
  • Tests first. Every task starts with a test that fails for the right reason.
  • Independent verification. verify runs in a new chat, ideally with another model. It checks every requirement against code and tests, and flags anything nobody asked for.

Small fixes take a lighter track, so a one-line bug does not need the whole cycle.

What happened on a real project

I used NodFirst 0.1.0 to build Shortz, a URL shortener, from init to a deployed app. It was one feature with 22 requirements and 32 tasks, built in one afternoon and evening in Cursor. It ended with 67 unit and integration tests and 52 end-to-end tests.

Before any code, analyze found two mandatory requirements that no acceptance criterion could prove: the limit on bulk creation and keeping URLs out of the logs. Implementation waited until both had one.

After the code, the first verify, run in a separate chat with Grok 4.7, found a security hole the implementer's tests had missed. The rate limiter trusted the first address in X-Forwarded-For, which the caller controls. The fix went through the normal path: a decision in the plan, new tasks, a new approval.

It did not end with a green tick. The third verification run said not verified, with 14 findings, 2 of them Critical under the kit's scale: dates shown in UTC instead of the user's time zone, and three dependencies not pinned to exact versions. I accepted the findings, closed the feature and wrote that down. The verdict stays not verified, and the full report is public.

The run also exposed gaps in the kit itself. There was no way to close a feature with accepted findings, and checks only a person could do blocked the verdict. Version 0.2.0 addressed both.

Try it

There is no program to install and no account to create.

  1. Copy everything inside kit/ into your project folder.
  2. Open the folder in your coding tool and write: follow nodfirst/playbooks/init.md A web app where a small gym books classes.
  3. Answer the questions, or say "your suggestion".

For an existing codebase, use nodfirst/playbooks/adopt.md instead. At the end the agent installs commands such as /nodfirst-specify and /nodfirst-verify ($nodfirst-… in Codex). /nodfirst-next tells you where you are and what to type next.

It is designed for Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and any agent that can read and edit files. The kit is in English, but your specs and conversation can be in any language.

Where it stands

NodFirst is at version 0.2.1, an early release. The core phases have been used on three projects. Several parts are less tested:

  • verify, design and the Cursor commands have been used on one project.
  • adopt, next, the Guided and Team profiles, and the command files for other tools have not been used yet.

The README keeps the full table.

Why not Spec Kit?

GitHub Spec Kit is the reference in this space, with a much larger ecosystem. If you are a developer who wants wide integrations and a big community, it is the mature choice. NodFirst makes other trade-offs: you copy a folder instead of installing a command-line tool, and approval gates are built into every playbook. It is aimed at people who want the agent to stop, explain and wait, including people who do not write code.

Tell me what breaks

The most useful contribution is a lesson from real use: what the agent got wrong, which rule was vague, which section was useless. Try it on something small and open an issue. I would especially like to know where the approval steps feel like too much.

NodFirst is MIT licensed: github.com/kaylit/nodfirst.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Neon vs Claude Opus 5.5: Price per Token Is Not Price per Task
articles.description: Google's Gemini 4 Neon is trending as the model that beat Claude Opus 5.5. The pitch is simple: a...
articles.body_html:
Google's Gemini 4 Neon is trending as the model that beat Claude Opus 5.5. The pitch is simple: a higher benchmark score at a lower price. If you pay for API calls, that sounds like an easy switch.

I'm a student who builds with these models and researches LLM hallucination, so I went through the numbers. The short version: Neon looks strong, but the headline comparison leaves out the thing that decides your bill.

The headline

Google launched Gemini 4 Neon on November 18, 2026. It sits between Gemini 4 Hydrogen (faster, cheaper) and Gemini 4 Carbon (slower, for the hardest work), with a context window of about one million tokens.

Gemini 4 Neon Claude Opus 5.5
Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 61 59
Input price (per 1M tokens) $3 $4
Output price (per 1M tokens) $15 $20

On paper, Neon is smarter and 25% cheaper per token. Here's what that table doesn't tell you.

1. The score depends on the thinking setting

Neon's 61 comes from its highest thinking level (xhigh). At its default level (high), Artificial Analysis puts it at 60. Opus 5.5's 59 is at its own maximum setting.

That's still a lead, just a smaller one. And thinking levels trade quality for time. Artificial Analysis reports Neon taking about 14.8 minutes per index task at high, and about 21.5 minutes at xhigh.

If you call the API with default settings, you're not getting the 61.

2. It's very verbose

This is the part that matters most for cost. On its index run, Artificial Analysis measured Neon producing about 283 million output tokens, against a median of about 65 million across models. They describe it as notably slow and very verbose.

Output tokens are the expensive side of the price sheet ($15 per million for Neon). A model that's cheaper per token but writes several times more tokens can end up costing the same or more per task.

That's why the useful number isn't price per token. It's cost per finished task.

3. When you measure per task, it still does well

To be fair to Neon, the per-task numbers that do exist look good:

  • On Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index, Neon (xhigh) scores 59 at about $6.86 per task, while Opus 5.5 (max) scores 58 at about $12.61 per task.
  • Caveat: those runs used different harnesses (Neon in Google's Antigravity CLI, Opus in Claude Code), so it's not a perfectly clean comparison.

So Neon may well be cheaper per task for coding agents. But that's because of how it performs on those tasks, not because the per-token price is lower. On a different workload, the verbosity could flip the result.

4. The hallucination claim has no number yet

Google says Neon makes fewer fabricated claims, especially unsupported claims about code or test results. For anyone running coding agents, that's the most valuable claim in the whole launch. An agent that says "tests pass" when they don't is worse than a slow one.

But I couldn't find a published number for it. The model card still lists hallucination as a general limitation. Until there's a measured rate, treat it as a claim.

5. Most of the benchmark table is Google's own

Google's launch table shows Neon ahead of Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol on most rows, with a few losses (FrontierCode 2.0 and Chartography, for example). Some rows are third-party, like Vals AI's index and Artificial Analysis. Many are Google's own runs, and the table doesn't always state which thinking level was used. Different sites even count the wins differently (16 of 19 rows vs 8 of 10 shared rows), depending on which rows they include.

How I'd actually decide

If you're thinking of switching, test it on your own work instead of trusting the leaderboard:

  1. Pick 10 to 20 real tasks from your own workload, not benchmark-style prompts.
  2. Run both models at the settings you'd actually use, not the maximum setting from the launch chart.
  3. Log input and output tokens per task, then multiply by each model's price. That gives you real cost per task.
  4. Grade the outputs, including whether either model claimed something that wasn't true (a passing test, an API that doesn't exist).
  5. Time them. A verbose model at xhigh can be slow enough to matter in an interactive tool.

Then compare cost per correct task. That's the only number that ends up on your bill.

Gemini 4 Neon might be the better choice for a lot of developers. The point is just that "61 vs 59, and cheaper" isn't enough to know.

Have you tried Neon on your own tasks yet? What did cost per task look like for you?

Sources:

  • OfficeChai, Gemini 4 Neon benchmarks: https://officechai.com/ai/gemini-4-neon-benchmarks/
  • AgentsPulse, Neon benchmarks and cost per task (citing Artificial Analysis): https://agentspulse.github.io/tutorials/gemini-4-neon-benchmarks/
  • LLM Stats, Neon launch breakdown: https://llm-stats.com/blog/research/gemini-4-neon-launch
  • CASRAI, launch and pricing: https://casrai.org/news/gemini-4-neon-launch-pricing-science-benchmarks-2026

I'm Veer, I write about AI, tech and society at SpaceRock. More of my work: veersolanki.in

articles.title: Rust Won't Train Your Model. It Runs Everything Around It.
articles.description: Tokenizers, Codex, Bun and now Anthropic's Messages API run on Rust. What it buys over...
articles.body_html:
Tokenizers, Codex, Bun and now Anthropic's Messages API run on Rust. What it buys over Python, C++, Go and Mojo, where it loses, and a new open-source tool that ports your hot path with receipts.

This article was first published on Medium. The canonical URL is https://medium.com/@r3dtuxedo/rust-wont-train-your-model-it-runs-everything-around-it-944db0f1dc1b.


The model stays where it is. The ring around it is what's moving.

TL;DR

  • Rust isn't replacing Python for training. It's taking the layer around the model: tokenizers, weight files, data frames, serving, and the agent CLIs you run every day.
  • The strongest evidence is fresh. Anthropic says its Messages API, rewritten from Python to Rust, uses about 70% less CPU per request and cut median time to first token by about 20%.
  • The honest catch: a Rust function called once per item through a language bridge can be slower than the original. Move the loop, not the leaf.
  • rust-anything by Erkam Yaman turns that into a workflow: profile, port one unit with your coding agent, and switch it on only when recorded behavior matches. It's 12 days old, so treat it as promising, not proven.

On 25 November, Anthropic published how it moved the Messages API from Python to Rust. Anthropic calls it the primary way customers, and its own apps like Claude Code, reach Claude. In August, Bun shipped 1.4, its first release written in Rust instead of Zig. And OpenAI's Codex CLI has been Rust since 2025.

None of these teams moved their research to Rust. They moved the part that runs on every request.

Python is where the model is born. Rust is increasingly where it gets served.

This piece looks at why, where the trade-offs bite, and one tool that makes a small, checked first step possible.

Where Rust already sits in the AI stack

Most people picture "AI code" as a notebook full of PyTorch. That layer is still Python, and the kernels under it are still mostly C++ and CUDA. Everything between the model and the user is a different story.


Where each language does the work today. Sources listed at the end.

A few of those are easy to miss because you use them from Python:

  • Hugging Face tokenizers is written in Rust and called from Python. The "fast" tokenizers in transformers are built on it.
  • safetensors stores tensors "safely (as opposed to pickle)" with zero-copy loading. Loading a pickle can run code. Loading a safetensors file can't.
  • Polars is "an analytical query engine written in Rust", and uv and Ruff are Rust tools for Python itself: a package manager and a linter. uv's own benchmarks claim it is 10 to 100x faster than pip.

Then there are the agent tools. When OpenAI announced the Codex CLI rewrite in May 2025, the reasons were specific: no Node.js requirement to install, native sandboxing bindings, "no runtime garbage collection, resulting in lower memory consumption", and a wire protocol other languages can extend. Today GitHub counts the Codex repository as almost entirely Rust.

Four reasons it keeps winning that layer

1. Overhead per request adds up at scale. Anthropic's write-up is unusually concrete. Each request is validated, turned into a prompt, tokenized and screened, and each reply is sorted into text, thinking and tool calls as it streams. "Python added overhead to every one of those steps each time it created an object, freed memory, or handed its work to the next task." Traffic grew roughly 1,800 times from early 2024 to fall 2026. At that volume, overhead per request is the bill.

2. Memory safety without a garbage collector. C++ gives you control and no safety net. Go and Java give you a safety net and a collector. Rust's compiler rejects use-after-free and double-free at build time. Google reports a 1000x lower memory-safety vulnerability density in Android's Rust code than in its C and C++, and Rust changes there had a 4x lower rollback rate and spent 25% less time in review. Bun's author gave the same reason for leaving Zig: in safe Rust, those bugs "are compiler errors".

3. One binary, no runtime. Candle, Hugging Face's Rust ML framework, states its goal plainly: "make serverless inference possible". Full frameworks like PyTorch are large and slow to start on a cluster, and Candle ships lightweight binaries. The same property is why Codex installs without Node.

4. It runs in the browser too. Candle's demos run Whisper, LLaMA2, T5 and Segment Anything entirely in the browser through WebAssembly. For edge or on-device inference, the same code compiles to a native binary and to WASM.

The compiler is a reviewer that never gets tired. That matters more now that agents write a lot of the code.

How it compares

Rust isn't the right answer everywhere. Here's the short version, as of late November 2026.

Language Best at in AI Memory safety Runtime cost Main catch
Python Research, training, glue; PyTorch and JAX live here Yes (GC) Interpreter and object overhead on every call The GIL is optional only in the free-threaded build (official since 3.14, not the default)
C++ Kernels, inference engines (llama.cpp), PyTorch's core No Lowest Memory bugs are your job
Go Network services and local runners (Ollama) Yes (GC) Low, with a collector Thin ML ecosystem; cgo for native libraries
Mojo GPU and accelerator kernels with Python-like syntax Safer than C++ by design, less proven Low Young: 1.0 and an open-source compiler only since August 2026
Rust Serving, tokenizers, data, agent CLIs, edge and WASM Yes, no GC Low Learning curve, compile times, few training libraries

The fair summary: if your problem is training a model, stay in Python. If it's a GPU kernel, look at C++/CUDA or Mojo. If it's the service, the tool or the pipeline that runs millions of times around the model, Rust has the best mix of speed and safety on offer.

The catch: the bridge has a toll

Here's the part most "rewrite it in Rust" posts skip. Anthropic didn't start with a full rewrite. It first rewrote only the output parser in Rust and called it from Python. That cut CPU by about 8 to 10%, but "each token now crossed between Python and Rust three times", and the gain didn't justify the complexity. The full rewrite of the request path is what got to about 70%.

rust-anything's own benchmark logs show the same effect on a small scale, and its FAQ says it bluntly: "Is Rust always faster? No." Its first Python, Go, Ruby and Java bridges sent every argument through JSON, which cost 10 to 50x more than the work itself. Even after rebuilding them, a Go function ported on its own ran at 0.04x of Go's speed, because Go was already fast and every call now crossed a boundary.


Same tool, same kind of code. Where the boundary sits decides the result. Per-call figures are geometric means from rust-anything's bench; batch figures compare all cores against one thread unless marked. Source: rust-anything docs, real-world.md and real-world-languages.md, Apple M4, read 28 Nov 2026.

A tiny function that V8, the JVM or Go runs in nanoseconds gets slower when every call crosses a bridge. Move the loop around it, so the data crosses once, and the picture flips: 5.3x on a single core for Fuse.js search, more with all cores. The lesson transfers to any Python service: port the hot path whole, not one leaf at a time.

rust-anything: port one piece, prove it matches

rust-anything is an open-source CLI by Erkam Yaman (MIT or Apache-2.0). It doesn't call a model itself. It's a toolkit your coding agent drives, and it works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode. Sources can be TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby, Java, C, PHP, C#, Kotlin or PowerShell.

The loop: analyze plans what to port, profile finds what's hot under a real workload, and go bridges the hottest function, records what the original returns, throws and prints, hands the port to your agent, then builds, diffs and gates it. gate means every recorded case matches, plus fmt, clippy, cargo test, an unsafe check and a check that the agent didn't paste recorded answers into the port. Only then does enable switch callers to Rust, and disable switches them back.

That's the same lesson as Anthropic's post, at the size of one function: generating the port is the easy part, and the recorded behavior of the original is the oracle. Anthropic's Rust API passed about 98% of its tests in April while only about a quarter of production inputs matched, and an audit of the ported tests found more than 100 weakened assertions.

Your tests tell you what you thought of. Recorded behavior tells you what the code actually does.

The report steps cost nothing to try. I installed 5.0.2 and pointed profile at the repo's own Python eval fixture with a small loop as the workload:

$ rust-anything profile . -- python3 work.py   # output trimmed
2359 ms in all; 62% of it in the repository's own code.

  Function       File                    Total  Self     Calls
  title_case     original/textkit.py:4   78%    1129 ms  200000
  format_number  original/textkit.py:16  13%    218 ms   200000

What to port
- title_case (78%): Hot and exported by original/: port it, then check rust-anything bench.

analyze on the same folder flagged the risks a port has to get right: five string-offset spots (Rust slices UTF-8 bytes, Python counts code points), dynamic typing and exceptions. No model was called and no file changed.

I wrapped both reports into a small read-only script that prints a shortlist and flags functions that are too cheap per call to port alone, the bridge toll from above:

https://gist.github.com/br4vesirrobin/1ef37e332bded8bc851210b4b582d258


Four questions before you rewrite anything.

What to watch with a 12-day-old tool

The repository was created on 16 November 2026 and had 10,993 stars, 894 forks and 60 contributors on 28 November, re-checked at 13:22 Berlin. That's a lot of attention for 12 days, and version 5.0.2 already. The good signs: the docs publish where Rust lost (the 0.56x result is on the project's own page), the status table separates "Verified" on real code (ESLint, Prettier, ffmpeg's libavutil, CPython's colorsys) from "Tested" on fixtures, and the evals page says "No results are published yet" rather than inventing a number. The author also offers paid migration consulting, which is fine, but worth knowing.

Start with analyze and profile. They're read-only. Let the agent port one unit, read the diff, and keep disable one command away.

The short version

Rust won't train your next model, and it doesn't need to. The value is in the layer that runs on every request: the tokenizer, the weight loader, the API server, the agent on your laptop. That's where garbage collection, interpreter overhead and memory bugs cost the most, and where Anthropic and OpenAI have already moved.

If you try it, start where it's measurable: one hot path, one recorded oracle, one switch you can flip back.

What's the one part of your AI stack you'd move first?

Sources

  • Anthropic, "Migrating our Messages API to Rust", 25 Nov 2026: https://www.anthropic.com/research/migrating-api-to-rust
  • OpenAI, "Codex CLI is Going Native", GitHub discussion #1174, 30 May 2025: https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/1174
  • Bun blog, "Rewriting Bun in Rust", 8 Jul 2026: https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust and "Bun 1.4", 20 Aug 2026: https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4
  • Google Security Blog, "Rust in Android: move fast and fix things", 13 Nov 2025: https://security.googleblog.com/2025/11/rust-in-android-move-fast-fix-things.html
  • Hugging Face candle README (goals, WASM demos): https://github.com/huggingface/candle
  • Hugging Face tokenizers: https://github.com/huggingface/tokenizers ; safetensors: https://github.com/huggingface/safetensors
  • Polars: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars ; uv (benchmarks): https://github.com/astral-sh/uv ; Ruff: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff
  • Python 3.14 What's New, PEP 779 (free-threaded build officially supported): https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html
  • Modular, "Mojo is now open source", 18 Aug 2026: https://www.modular.com/blog/mojo-open-source
