articles.title: Designing Low-Latency Realtime Sync with WebSockets, CRDTs, and PartyKit
articles.description: Most developers building their first collaborative feature start with a naive WebSocket architecture:...
articles.body_html:
Most developers building their first collaborative feature start with a naive WebSocket architecture: when a user drags an element or types a character, the client emits an event payload, and the server broadcasts that exact payload to every other connected socket.

This pattern collapses the moment two users perform concurrent actions or when a high-latency network delays a single packet. You quickly encounter race conditions, clobbered state, cursor rubber-banding, and desynchronized sessions.

To build software that feels as resilient and fluid as Figma or Google Docs, you need to decouple transport from consistency. Here is how modern multiplayer architectures achieve Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) using CRDTs and edge-based WebSocket workers.

Why Operational Transformation Fell Behind CRDTs

Historically, collaborative tools used Operational Transformation (OT). OT relies on a centralized coordinator to transform operation indices based on logical timestamps. If client A deletes character 3 while client B inserts at character 1, the server rewrites client A's operation index before broadcasting.

While OT powers Google Docs, it requires complex centralized sequence servers and makes peer-to-peer or multi-region edge deployment virtually impossible.

Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) solve this mathematically through join-semilattices. A valid CRDT satisfies three core algebraic properties:

  1. Associativity: (a ⊔ b) ⊔ c = a ⊔ (b ⊔ c). Updates can be batched in arbitrary network frames without altering the final state.
  2. Commutativity: a ⊔ b = b ⊔ a. Updates can arrive out of order over UDP/WebSockets without diverging.
  3. Idempotence: a ⊔ a = a. Retrying dropped network packets produces zero state corruption.

Modern libraries like Yjs optimize this by structuring updates into an append-only doubly linked item list indexed in a linear memory array (StructStore), making CRDT updates fast and lightweight.

Pattern 1: Edge-Native Multiplayer Rooms with PartyKit

Instead of managing long-lived, memory-heavy Node.js WebSocket containers that require sticky sessions and Redis pub/sub bridges, edge runtimes like PartyKit let you run stateful rooms directly on Cloudflare Workers close to your users.

Here is a minimal PartyKit server that coordinates binary Yjs document synchronization:

import type { Party, Room, Server } from "partykit/server";
import { onConnect } from "y-partykit";

export default class RealtimeRoomServer implements Server {
  constructor(readonly room: Room) {}

  async onConnect(conn: Party.Connection, ctx: Party.ConnectionContext) {
    // Setup Yjs binary protocol binding over the edge WebSocket
    return onConnect(conn, this.room, {
      persist: {
        mode: "history",
        // Automatically snapshot document state to durable storage
        async save(doc) {
          await this.room.storage.put("yjs-doc", doc);
        },
        async load() {
          return (await this.room.storage.get<Uint8Array>("yjs-doc")) ?? null;
        }
      }
    });
  }
}

Pattern 2: Decoupling Document State from Ephemeral Presence

A common architectural bug in collaborative canvases is writing cursor coordinates directly to the persistent CRDT document. This rapidly bloats your persistent CRDT history with megabytes of transient mouse trails.

Always isolate document state (shapes, text, nodes) from awareness state (cursors, selections, active users). Yjs provides the Awareness protocol specifically for volatile, lossy sync:

import * as Y from "yjs";
import YPartyKitProvider from "y-partykit/provider";

const doc = new Y.Doc();
const provider = new YPartyKitProvider(
  "my-party.project.partykit.dev",
  "canvas-room-101",
  doc
);

// 1. Persistent Shared Data: Monitored & Synced via CRDT
const sharedShapes = doc.getMap("canvas-shapes");
sharedShapes.observe((event) => {
  renderCanvas(sharedShapes.toJSON());
});

// 2. Ephemeral Presence: High-frequency, never saved to disk
const awareness = provider.awareness;

window.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  awareness.setLocalStateField("cursor", {
    x: e.clientX,
    y: e.clientY,
    user: "Alex",
    color: "#ff0055"
  });
});

awareness.on("change", () => {
  const states = awareness.getStates();
  renderLiveCursors(states);
});

Pattern 3: Local Optimistic Rendering with Automatic Rollbacks

To ensure zero input lag, mutations must immediately apply locally without waiting for the server roundtrip. Because Yjs transactions run synchronously against local memory structures, you can apply updates locally first:

doc.transact(() => {
  sharedShapes.set("rect-42", {
    type: "rectangle",
    x: 120,
    y: 240,
    color: "blue"
  });
}, "local-origin");

If another user deleted rect-42 milliseconds before your packet reached the edge, the join-semilattice automatically resolves the conflict deterministically. No manual reconciliation scripts or UI rollbacks are needed.

Level Up Your Realtime Engineering Stack

Building enterprise-grade multiplayer systems requires going far beyond basic pub/sub. You need to handle reconnection storms, room hibernation, selective delta compression, custom undo/redo stacks across multiple collaborators, and offline-first storage sync.

If you want the complete implementation guide, check out The Realtime Collaborative App Engine: WebSockets, CRDTs, PartyKit & Yjs Playbook ($29).

The playbook provides end-to-end production blueprints, including:

  • In-depth breakdowns of the YATA algorithm and StructStore memory layouts
  • Production-ready PartyKit and Cloudflare Durable Object room templates
  • Multi-client undo/redo managers that ignore other users' changes
  • Binary protocol decoders for minimal WebSocket bandwidth consumption
  • Scalable presence clustering for 1,000+ concurrent viewers per room

articles.title: Black for C++: what if your indentation was your syntax tree?
articles.description: A formatting convention that makes nested C++ expressions readable, and a formatter that applies it.
articles.body_html:
I recently wrote a line of C++ that took me three passes to read. It was not clever code. It was an ordinary constructor initializer list.

Display::Display(Keyboard &keyboard, int output, const Vector &position,
                 const Vector &size, const Vector &expandTo, Screen screen)
    : keyboard_(keyboard), output_{output}, screen_{screen},
      cursor_(enter(position)), terminalSize_{terminalSize()},
      foreground_{RgbWhite}, background_{RgbNone}, attributes_{},
      position_{screen == Screen::alternate? Vector{0, 0}
                : position == VectorMin    ? cursor_
                                            : position},
      maxSize_{min(expandTo == VectorMax? terminalSize_ : expandTo,
                   screen == Screen::alternate
                       ? terminalSize_
                       : Vector{toDim(terminalSize_.x() - position_.x()),
                                terminalSize_.y()})},
      text_(Null, size == VectorMin ? Vector{1, 1} : min(size, maxSize_)) {
  cursor(false);
  makeRoom(text_.height());
  keyboard.displayOffset(position_);
}

I wrote this, and I still had to trace the nested conditional with my finger.

Alignment optimizes for width, not structure

Most C++ formatting is built around a column budget. Lines wrap, continuations align to an opening bracket or get a fixed indent, and the result is judged by how much fits.

That answers a real question: how wide can a line be? It does not answer the question I have while reading: what belongs to what?

A nested conditional is where this shows up worst. The ? and : end up scattered across the line, and recovering the tree means counting columns and tracing back to the nearest operator.

position_ = screen == Screen::alternate
              ? Vector{0, 0}
              : position == VectorMin
                  ? cursor_
                  : position;

Two levels of nesting, and the indentation records the author's guess about where the operators looked best.

The rule

Structured indentation replaces the guess with four rules that follow the syntax:

  1. A context that does not fit on a line opens with its opening token last on the line, and indents its contents.
  2. It closes with a dedented closing token.
  3. A context that has an opening token but no closing token — the ? in a ternary, the : after a constructor's parameter list — indents after that token and dedents when the context ends.
  4. Items in an indented block are written one per line.

The same expression, formatted by those rules:

position_ =
  screen == Screen::alternate?
    Vector{0, 0}:
    position == VectorMin?
      cursor_:
      position;

The = ends the first line, and the initializer is indented under it. The first ? ends the condition and opens the branch below. The : ends that branch, and the alternative starts at the same indentation as the branch above it. The second ? opens another level because it belongs to that alternative.

The visual line

The result is what the spec calls a visual line: the contents of a context form a contiguous block, and the token that closes it returns to the column of its opener. Inside a block, every line at the same indentation belongs to the same context, and the end of that context is visible at the margin.

This is the one thing a formatter must not break. Keep the visual line intact and the shape of the code survives — at any depth.

One expression, four levels

Here is a single one-line expression, formatted by two tools. Both outputs came from running the tools on the input; they are not illustrations.

Input:

auto names = collect(transform(filter(users, [](const User & user) { return user.active; }), [](const User & user) { return user.name; }));

clang-format, default LLVM style:

auto names = collect(
    transform(filter(users, [](const User &user) { return user.active; }),
              [](const User &user) { return user.name; }));

cxxformat 0.1.0:

auto names = collect(
  transform(
    filter(
      users,
      [](const User & user) {
        return user.active;
      }
    ),
    [](const User & user) {
      return user.name;
    }
  )
);

The clang-format version is shorter, and it is not wrong. But the nesting is carried by alignment columns, and the lambda bodies are squeezed inline. To see that the second lambda is an argument of transform rather than of filter, you follow an alignment across three lines.

In the second version every context is a block. collect( owns everything up to its closing ), transform( owns its two arguments, filter( owns its two, and each lambda owns its body. You can read the bottom of the expression and know exactly which construct you are in.

You might object that clang-format can be configured closer. AlignAfterOpenBracket: BlockIndent and BinPackArguments: false do produce more block-like output; I tried. It still packs the outer call and closes with )); on one line, so the blocks never fully separate.

Depth is not the enemy

The same effect applies to control flow once a header or a body is an expression that has to break:

void render(const std::vector<Row> & rows) {
  for (std::size_t row = 0; row < rows.size(); ++row) {
    for (std::size_t column = 0; column < rows[row].size(); ++column) {
      if (
        rows[row][column].visible
          && rows[row][column].width > 0
          && rows[row][column].x + rows[row][column].width <= width
      ) {
        draw(rows[row][column].x, rows[row][column].y, rows[row][column].glyph);
      }
    }
  }
}

The left edge has four positions: 2 for the function body, 4 for the outer loop, 6 for the inner loop, 8 for the if body. Apart from the && continuations, no line starts anywhere else. The if ( header is a block too, so the condition is not wrapped into an aligned sentence; the closing ) returns to the column of the if. The && lines are indented one level past the first operand, because there the operator leads the line and the operand follows.

I am not arguing that this function should stay nested. I am arguing that you can see what it does. The nesting is on the page, not in your head.

Formatting pressure

Every width-limited formatter carries an unwritten rule: keep the expression short enough that the wrap stays readable. You internalize it without noticing. You add a temporary to shorten a line. You split a condition into two ifs with a boolean. You extract a function that exists mainly to give a call a shorter name.

Some of those changes are good. Some exist because the formatter made the direct version ugly, not because the direct version was unclear.

That is the real argument for structured indentation. It does not make complex code simple — nothing does. It makes complexity visible, so the formatter stops being the reason you avoid it. You can write the nested version, see its shape, and then decide whether it deserves to stay. The decision moves back to you.

Python already works this way

If this looks familiar, it is because it is how Black formats a call that does not fit:

result = some_function(
    first_argument,
    second_argument,
)

The opening bracket ends the line, the arguments are indented, and the closing bracket is dedented. If your Python projects use Black, you have been reading structured indentation without calling it that.

Black makes different choices elsewhere. A broken conditional expression starts if and else on new lines, where this convention keeps ? and : as line-ending delimiters. Black also normalizes quotes and string prefixes; structured indentation only changes whitespace. The central rule is the same, and that is what makes the idea credible rather than exotic: it is already in one of the most widely used formatters in the world.

A formatter that applies it

I wanted to use this on real C++ code, so I wrote cxxformat. The command is c++format. It parses with tree-sitter, rewrites whitespace only, and preserves every token, including comments and string literals. If the parser reports a syntax error, it refuses to write the file unless you pass --force.

brew install jwezel/cxxformat/cxxformat

c++format --diff src/main.cpp   # inspect the proposed changes
c++format --check src include   # exit 1 if formatting is needed
c++format -i src include        # write in place

The command line borrows the useful parts of clang-format and Black: stdout by default, -i for in-place writes, --check and --diff for CI, stdin support, YAML configuration, and --dump-config for a documented starting point.

In CI it is one step:

- name: Check formatting
  run: c++format --check --diff src include

Formatting is idempotent, and the test suite verifies that against golden fixtures.

What it costs

The vertical space is real. A nested expression can grow from four lines to ten. I think that is a fair trade because I read code far more often than I write it, and folding covers the case where I need density. Not everyone will agree, and that is a legitimate objection.

The first diff on an existing codebase is large. So is the first run of gofmt or Black. After that, a diff shows a structural change because the structure changed.

The formatter only touches what it understands. Code inside #if/#else branches is preserved rather than formatted, macros can confuse the parser, and comments are never reflowed. Some constructs are still handled conservatively. Formatting is checked against tree-sitter, not a compiler AST, so review the diff before committing. The README lists the rest of the limitations instead of hiding them.

It is also v0.1.0, MIT licensed, and early.

Try it

  • Specification: https://structured-indentation.org
  • Formatter and installation: https://github.com/jwezel/cxxformat

If you try it, format one directory, read the diff, then decide. I am more interested in where the output is wrong than in whether you like the style.

One question for the comments: the trailing ? and : are the part people either like immediately or reject on sight. Do they read as structure to you, or do they look like a typo?

articles.title: Your Tabs Are Talking Behind Your Back
articles.description: Imagine you log out of an app in one tab.  You switch to another tab. Same app. Still logged in,...
articles.body_html:
Imagine you log out of an app in one tab.

You switch to another tab. Same app. Still logged in, apparently.

You click Edit. The form opens. You type. You click Save.

And only then does the server answer with a 401, and your changes are gone.

No line of code is wrong, exactly. Each tab is living in its own little world, and nobody told the second tab that the party was over.

The browser has plenty of ways to fix that. Eight of them, by my count, and from a distance they all look alike. This article is the map: what each one does, who it talks to, and when I'd reach for it.

(Spoiler: for the logout, it's BroadcastChannel. But it isn't always the answer.)

1. One question sorts them all: who is talking to whom?

Line these APIs up and they look like a pile of things that all send messages. The pile gets much smaller once you ask one question: who is on each end of the conversation?

Once you know who needs to hear the message, you're usually down to one or two candidates.

Start with the audience, and the right API mostly picks itself.

2. What they have in common

  • They're event-driven. You never ask "any news?". You add a listener and wait for a message (or storage) event. Your code reacts instead of polling.
  • Most are same-origin only. BroadcastChannel, SharedWorker, Service Worker and the storage APIs all stay inside one origin. Only postMessage, WebSocket and SSE can cross origins, which is why they come with origin checks or CORS attached.
  • The local ones never leave the device. A BroadcastChannel message in your laptop's browser will never reach your phone. For that you need a server in the middle.
  • Structured clone vs. strings only. postMessage on channels, workers and windows uses the structured clone algorithm, so objects, arrays, Map, Date and Blob arrive as real copies. Storage, WebSocket text frames and SSE give you strings, so get comfortable with JSON.stringify.

That last point is where most surprises come from. Functions and DOM nodes can't be cloned, and trying throws a DataCloneError. The browser is happy to copy your data, just not your entire app.

Same origin and same device cover most cases. Everything else needs a server or an explicit origin check.

3. The cast, one by one

Here's each one, with a few lines of code and the job it's good at.

BroadcastChannel: the named radio station

Everyone who tunes in to the same channel name hears every message. The sender doesn't hear itself, and nothing is stored, so a tab that opens later misses everything said before it arrived.

Use it for: keeping same-origin tabs in sync. Logout, theme changes, "this item was updated", "this notification was read".

window.postMessage: the direct phone line

You call one specific window, iframe or popup. It's the only local option that works across origins, so it comes with two rules: always pass an exact targetOrigin when you send, and always check event.origin when you receive. Skip the check, and any page that gets hold of your window can send you whatever it likes. It will.

Use it for: iframes, popups (OAuth and payment windows are the classics) and embedded widgets from another origin.

SharedWorker: the roommate who holds the one connection

A SharedWorker is a script that runs in the background, separate from any page, and every tab of your site connects to the same copy of it. It stays alive as long as at least one of those tabs is open, and it remembers whatever you keep in its variables the whole time. Each tab talks to it through its own port, and the worker keeps a list of them. The classic use: the worker opens one WebSocket and passes every message on to all the tabs.

On the page side, it's new SharedWorker('/cart-worker.js').port.onmessage = .... Two catches. A closed tab doesn't tell the worker it left, so a real version has to clean up dead ports. And mobile support has been patchy for years: Chrome for Android only caught up recently, and some mobile browsers still don't have it. Check your audience before you rely on it.

Use it for: one expensive resource (a socket, a big cache) shared by every tab.

Service Worker: the bouncer who naps

A Service Worker is also a background script, but its real job is the network. Every request from the pages it controls goes through it first, and it decides whether to go to the server or answer from a cache. That's how offline mode works. It can even wake up when no tab is open at all, for example to receive a push notification. Talking to tabs is a side feature: clients.matchAll() lists the open pages it controls, and you postMessage each one.

The catch: the browser stops it whenever it's idle and starts it again for the next event. Anything you keep in a variable is gone after the nap. A goldfish with a very good network connection. So state belongs in IndexedDB or the Cache API, not in memory.

Pages listen with navigator.serviceWorker.onmessage.

So the difference in one sentence: a SharedWorker lives with your open tabs and remembers, while a Service Worker lives with your site, works even with no tabs open, and forgets.

Use it for: push notifications, offline sync, and anything that has to happen while no page is in focus.

localStorage and sessionStorage: the shelf (and its doorbell)

These are storage, not messaging. Strings only, about 5 MB per origin, and every read and write is synchronous. localStorage is shared by all tabs and survives a browser restart. sessionStorage belongs to one tab. A tab opened from it (or duplicated, in most browsers) starts with a copy, and from then on the two go their separate ways.

The shelf does have a doorbell, though. When localStorage changes, every other same-origin tab gets a storage event. Before BroadcastChannel, that was the trick for cross-tab messages: write a key, and the other tabs react. It fires only in the other tabs, never in the one that made the change. It still works fine. It just needs a lot more paperwork than the job requires.

Use it for: the last-known state that should still be there after a reload. The doorbell is a free bonus when you already write the value there, or a fallback for very old browsers. For plain messages, BroadcastChannel is simpler.

WebSocket and SSE: the long-distance calls

Everything above stays on one device. When an update has to reach your other laptop, your phone, or another user, it has to go through a server.

WebSocket is a two-way line. SSE (EventSource) only sends from server to browser, but it reconnects automatically and runs over plain HTTP, which makes it much simpler to operate.

Use it for: chat and collaboration (WebSocket), feeds and notifications (SSE).

That's the whole cast.

Each tool is best at one job, and most bugs come from asking it to do a different one.

4. Picking one

Here's the decision list I go through. Start at the top, and the first "yes" wins.

Storage answers "where does the data live", not "who gets told". So if you land on the last box, you probably still need one of the boxes above it. Nobody has ever been notified by a shelf.

The first yes wins, and storage is never that yes on its own.

5. The real-world combo

In practice, one tool is rarely enough. A setup that shows up again and again has three parts:

  • One connection. A SharedWorker holds the WebSocket. Where SharedWorker isn't available, one tab becomes the leader and holds it instead. The Web Locks API (navigator.locks) is a tidy way to pick that tab.
  • One fan-out. Whoever holds the socket passes every update on through a BroadcastChannel, so all tabs hear it at once.
  • One memory. The last-known state goes into localStorage, so a tab that opens later, or reloads, starts from the right place instead of an empty screen.

Each part covers a gap in the others. BroadcastChannel forgets everything. localStorage remembers but never announces. The WebSocket knows about other devices, but it shouldn't be opened ten times for ten tabs. Ten tabs, ten sockets, one very confused backend.

The logout from the beginning fits right in. A logout in one tab goes out on the channel, every other tab redirects to the login page, and nobody gets to fill in a form that's already doomed.

I built the fan-out part for notifications in a real app: new notifications arrive over SSE, and when you read one, BroadcastChannel tells your other tabs so their badges update too. It gets its own article, Mark as Read, Everywhere, with the parts this overview skips: the message shape, what the sending tab does, and how to test it.

Connect once, fan out locally, and keep the last state on the shelf.

Final thoughts

Eight APIs sounds like a lot, but they come down to three ideas.

Ask who's listening. Another tab, another origin, another device. That one question removes most of the options before you write any code.

Messages and memory are different jobs. Channels and workers deliver news. Storage keeps it. Most real setups need one of each.

Local stays local. Anything that has to reach another device needs a server, no matter how well your tabs get along.

Your tabs are going to talk behind your back anyway. You might as well decide what they say.

articles.title: Your cookie banner says "Reject". Here's how to check if anything listens
articles.description: When we loaded 876 websites from 14 EU countries without touching the cookie banner, 55 % of them had...
articles.body_html:
When we loaded 876 websites from 14 EU countries without touching the
cookie banner, 55 % of them had already sent requests to analytics or
advertising services. Most of those sites had a perfectly normal-looking
banner. The banner was there; it just wasn't connected to everything it
was supposed to hold back.

You can't see that by looking at the page. You can see it in about five
minutes in the network tab, and if you want to repeat it after every
deploy, in about 40 lines of Playwright. Both below.

The manual check (5 minutes)

  1. Open a private window. An old consent cookie hides everything.
  2. Disable ad blockers and privacy extensions for this test. They block the very requests you're looking for.
  3. Open DevTools (F12) before you load the page. In the Network tab, tick "Preserve log" and "Disable cache".
  4. Load the site and don't touch the banner.
  5. Filter for the usual suspects: google-analytics, googletagmanager, doubleclick, facebook, clarity.ms, hotjar, tiktok, linkedin, fonts.googleapis. In Chrome, the "3rd-party requests" filter helps you spot the ones you didn't expect.
  6. Check Application → Cookies and Local Storage. _ga, _gcl_au, _fbp, _hj* before any click is a red flag.
  7. Now click "Reject", reload, and open a second page. Do the same filters again.

That second pass matters more than people think. Many setups behave on
the first page view and leak on the second, or ignore "Reject" because
the tag fires on "All pages" instead of on the consent event.

One Google-specific detail: in Consent Mode "advanced", Google tags load
before consent and send pings with gcs=G100 (denied). That's how the
mode is designed. If you want zero requests to Google before consent,
you need "basic" mode, where the tags don't load at all until someone
agrees.

Where the leaks usually come from

From what we saw across those 876 sites, it's rarely the banner itself:

  • Scripts pasted into the theme header (pixel snippets, "header scripts" fields in the theme settings). They run before any consent tool gets a say.
  • Tag Manager triggers set to "All Pages" without a consent condition.
  • Plugins and apps that inject their own tracking, especially on WordPress and Shopify.
  • Embeds: YouTube, Vimeo, Google Maps without a click-to-load placeholder.
  • Google Fonts from Google's servers. 57 % of the sites loaded them before consent, usually through the theme or a page builder, not because anyone added them on purpose. Each request sends the visitor's IP to Google.

When something shows up early, the Initiator column in the network tab
tells you which file loaded it. That's usually the fastest way to the
plugin or snippet responsible.

Automating it with Playwright

Doing the manual check once is fine. Doing it after every plugin update
is where it falls apart. Here's a minimal script that loads a page in a
fresh context, records third-party requests before any click, clicks a
reject button, and records again:

import { chromium } from "playwright";

const url = process.argv[2];
const host = new URL(url).hostname.replace(/^www\./, "");
const TRACKERS = /google-analytics|googletagmanager|doubleclick|facebook|clarity\.ms|hotjar|tiktok|linkedin|fonts\.googleapis/;

const thirdParty = (reqs) =>
  [...new Set(reqs.map((r) => new URL(r).hostname))]
    .filter((h) => !h.endsWith(host));

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const context = await browser.newContext(); // fresh: no consent cookie
const page = await context.newPage();

let seen = [];
page.on("request", (r) => seen.push(r.url()));

await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });
const before = thirdParty(seen);

// Common wording; extend for your banner and language.
const reject = page.getByRole("button", { name: /reject|decline|deny|only necessary|ablehnen/i }).first();
if (await reject.isVisible().catch(() => false)) {
  await reject.click();
  seen = [];
  await page.reload({ waitUntil: "networkidle" });
} else {
  console.log("No reject button found on the first layer.");
}
const after = thirdParty(seen);

console.log("Before consent:", before.filter((h) => TRACKERS.test(h)));
console.log("After reject:  ", after.filter((h) => TRACKERS.test(h)));
await browser.close();

Run it with node check.mjs https://your-site.example. Two empty lists
is what you want. A non-empty "before" list means something loads ahead
of the banner; a non-empty "after" list means "Reject" isn't wired to it.

Limits worth knowing:

  • The regex is a starting point, not a tracker database. Print the full before list once and look at every host you don't recognise.
  • Banners differ. Some put "Reject" behind "Settings", some use links instead of buttons, some live in an iframe. If the script says it found no reject button, look at the banner by hand: a missing reject option on the first layer is a finding in itself (43 % of the banners in our sample had none).
  • Bot protection can serve a different page to headless browsers. If results look odd, compare with a normal browser before trusting them.
  • Server-side tracking doesn't show up in the browser at all.

What I ended up building

I kept running variations of that script on more and more sites, and it
grew into a scanner that does the full version: it checks several pages,
finds the reject button in the usual banner tools, confirms suspicious
results with an ordinary browser, and names the file that loaded each
service plus the setting to change in your consent tool. The first
report is free and needs no sign-up, if you want to compare it with what
your own script finds:
https://konformia.at/en?q=devto-blocking

The study with method and limits is here:
https://konformia.at/en/cookie-study?q=devto-blocking

If your banner breaks the script in an interesting way, tell me in the
comments. Those are the cases I learn the most from.

articles.title: Parsing ZIP Playable Ads in Browser Memory with Native DecompressionStream & Validating 6 Mobile Ad Networks
articles.description: When you ship HTML5 playable ads for mobile game user acquisition (UA), the gameplay loop is only...
articles.body_html:
When you ship HTML5 playable ads for mobile game user acquisition (UA), the gameplay loop is only half the engineering battle. The other half is surviving six ad networks whose static packaging rules actively contradict each other.

A build that uploads cleanly to AppLovin fails Unity Ads. A build that passes Google Ads fails Meta and Mintegral. And because studio art assets are usually under strict NDA, uploading unreleased game bundles to a random third-party web server just to check packaging rules is a non-starter.

Here is how we extracted our static compliance engine into a 100% browser-local, zero-dependency HTML5 Playable Ad Validator that audits both single-file .html and .zip archives directly in browser memory—and the exact network quirks it catches.

1. The 6-Network Static Packaging Matrix

Every major mobile ad network enforces a different mix of file formats, size caps, SDK hooks, and markup constraints:

Ad Network Format & Cap Required SDK / CTA Hook Common Rejection Traps
AppLovin (MAX / Axon) Single HTML, <= 5 MB mraid.js, mraid.open(), viewableChange, audioVolumeChange Missing mraid.js, external fonts/CDNs, zero-interaction CTA triggers
Unity Ads (LevelPlay) Minified Single HTML, <= 5 MB Host-injected MRAID 3.0 + mraid.open() Bundling <script src="mraid.js"> (Unity injects it!), unminified HTML, non-store URLs
Meta (FB / Audience Network) Single HTML, <= 2 MB FbPlayableAd.onCTAClick() Including any MRAID reference or window.open(), exceeding 2 MB
Google Ads (App Campaigns) ZIP, <= 5 MB exitapi.js, ExitApi.exit(), ad.orientation meta Self-closing SVG tags (<rect ... />), broken relative CSS/HTML paths
Mintegral (Mindworks) Base64 ZIP, <= 5 MB gameReady(), gameStart(), gameClose(), window.install() ZIP basename must be [a-zA-Z0-9_] matching <name>/<name>.html, zero loose image/audio files
TikTok / Pangle ZIP, <= 5 MB playable-sdk.js, openAppStore() Missing or malformed root config.json (playable_orientation must be 0, 1, or 2)

For reference, skipping multi-megabyte WebGL engine wrappers in favor of vanilla Canvas + esbuild AST minification keeps our showcase playables on FirstTap Lab between 232 KB (ZIP) and 435 KB (Single HTML)—well under Meta’s 2 MB ceiling for near-instant WebView startup on mid-tier Android devices.

2. Unpacking .zip Playables in Browser Memory with Zero Dependencies

To inspect Google Ads, Mintegral, and TikTok ZIP deliverables locally without pulling in JSZip or touching a backend server, we wrote a compact ZIP Central Directory reader directly over DataView paired with the browser’s native DecompressionStream("deflate-raw"):

async function inflateRawBytes(u8) {
  const ds = new DecompressionStream("deflate-raw");
  const writer = ds.writable.getWriter();
  writer.write(u8);
  writer.close();
  return new Uint8Array(await new Response(ds.readable).arrayBuffer());
}

async function parseZip(arrayBuffer) {
  const view = new DataView(arrayBuffer);
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(arrayBuffer);

  // Locate End of Central Directory (0x06054b50)
  let eocd = -1;
  for (let i = bytes.length - 22; i >= Math.max(0, bytes.length - 65558); i--) {
    if (view.getUint32(i, true) === 0x06054b50) { eocd = i; break; }
  }
  if (eocd === -1) throw new Error("Invalid ZIP archive");

  const total = view.getUint16(eocd + 10, true);
  let ptr = view.getUint32(eocd + 16, true);
  const dec = new TextDecoder("utf-8");
  const entries = {};
  const names = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < total; i++) {
    if (view.getUint32(ptr, true) !== 0x02014b50) break;
    const method = view.getUint16(ptr + 10, true);
    const compSize = view.getUint32(ptr + 20, true);
    const nameLen = view.getUint16(ptr + 28, true);
    const extraLen = view.getUint16(ptr + 30, true);
    const commentLen = view.getUint16(ptr + 32, true);
    const localOff = view.getUint32(ptr + 42, true);
    const name = dec.decode(bytes.subarray(ptr + 46, ptr + 46 + nameLen));
    ptr += 46 + nameLen + extraLen + commentLen;
    names.push(name);

    if (name.endsWith("/") || !/\.(?:html?|css|js|json|svg|txt)$/i.test(name)) continue;

    const lNameLen = view.getUint16(localOff + 26, true);
    const lExtraLen = view.getUint16(localOff + 28, true);
    const dataStart = localOff + 30 + lNameLen + lExtraLen;
    const slice = bytes.subarray(dataStart, dataStart + compSize);

    entries[name] = method === 0
      ? dec.decode(slice)
      : method === 8
        ? dec.decode(await inflateRawBytes(slice))
        : "";
  }
  return { names, entries };
}

Once unpacked in memory, the validator resolves every relative HTML src/href and CSS url()/@import against the exact entry directory so broken ZIP paths get flagged before upload.

3. Catching Hidden Network Calls & Self-Closing SVG Bugs

Two rejection causes trip up developers constantly:

  1. Google Ads self-closing SVG geometry: Google’s HTML5 parser rejects self-closing SVG tags like <rect x="0" y="0" width="100" height="100" />. Checking explicitly for: 
   /<(?:rect|ellipse|circle|path|line|polygon|polyline|stop|use)\b[^>]*\/>/gi

catches them instantaneously so you can emit explicit closing tags (<rect ...></rect>).

  1. Stray fetch() / XMLHttpRequest / sendBeacon() inside sandboxed WebViews: Running a naive regex over JS source causes false positives whenever comments mention fetch(). A tiny character-level scanner that respects single quotes, double quotes, template literals, and // / /* ... */ comments strips comments cleanly before scanning for forbidden runtime network calls.

4. Don’t Forget Runtime MRAID Hygiene

Passing static archive validation catches ~90% of upload-portal rejections, but behavioral MRAID bugs still kill live campaigns if you don’t test them:

  • Track hostReady, hostViewable, and docVisible independently; only tick the game loop when all three are true.
  • Never call mraid.getCurrentPosition() while mraid.getState() === "loading".
  • Respond immediately to mraid.sizeChange(w, h) on orientation changes rather than relying only on window.resize.
  • Gate AudioContext unlock strictly on the first genuine pointer gesture and respect host audioVolumeChange.

Try It Free (Zero Uploads, 3 One-Click Test Samples)

You can drop your own .html or .zip playable bundle—or click one of the 3 built-in sample files (Clean AppLovin PASS, Broken Meta HTML, Broken Google SVG/ExitApi)—directly at:

  • Free 6-Network Playable Ad Validator: https://firsttaplab.com/tools/playable-ad-validator/
  • Live Interactive Playable Demos & Simulator: https://firsttaplab.com/

If there is another mobile ad network spec you regularly get burned by (ironSource, Liftoff/Vungle, Snapchat, etc.), let me know in the comments and I will add its ruleset next!

articles.title: Turning an HLS stream into an MP4 inside a Chrome extension (MV3 lessons learned)
articles.description: I recently shipped a Chrome extension that saves online course lessons as MP4 files. The video side...
articles.body_html:
I recently shipped a Chrome extension that saves online course lessons as MP4 files. The video side turned out to be the hard part: the lessons are HLS streams, and Manifest V3 doesn't make big binary jobs easy. Here are the problems I hit and what worked, in case you're building anything similar.

The shape of the problem

An HLS lesson isn't one file. The player loads a master playlist (.m3u8), picks a quality, then fetches a few hundred 2–6 second segments (MPEG-TS or fMP4). Often audio is a separate rendition. To give the user one .mp4 you have to:

  1. find the right playlist,
  2. download every segment (fast, but without hammering the host),
  3. remux video + audio into an MP4 container,
  4. hand the result to chrome.downloads.

1. Finding the playlist: webRequest, not page scraping

The cleanest signal is the player's own network traffic. A chrome.webRequest.onBeforeRequest listener (read-only, no blocking) sees the .m3u8 URL the moment the player asks for it:

chrome.webRequest.onBeforeRequest.addListener((d) => {
  if (/\.m3u8(\?|$)/.test(d.url)) onCaptured(d.tabId, d.url, d.initiator);
}, { urls: ['https://*.example-video-host.com/*'] });

Keep the host list tight. Reviewers (and users) look at it.

2. Some hosts check Referer / Origin

Fetching segments from the extension gave me 403s, because the CDN expected requests to come from the course site. declarativeNetRequest session rules fix that without broad permissions:

await chrome.declarativeNetRequest.updateSessionRules({
  addRules: [{
    id: ruleId, priority: 1,
    action: { type: 'modifyHeaders', requestHeaders: [
      { header: 'referer', operation: 'set', value: 'https://www.example-course-site.com/' },
      { header: 'origin',  operation: 'set', value: 'https://www.example-course-site.com' },
    ]},
    condition: { urlFilter: '||example-video-host.com/', tabIds: [chrome.tabs.TAB_ID_NONE],
                 initiatorDomains: [chrome.runtime.id] },
  }],
});

tabIds: [TAB_ID_NONE] + initiatorDomains: [chrome.runtime.id] means the rule only touches the extension's own requests, never the user's browsing.

3. The service worker can't do the heavy lifting

An MV3 service worker can be killed after ~30 s idle and has no DOM. Holding 500 MB of segments there is a bad idea. The fix is an offscreen document:

await chrome.offscreen.createDocument({
  url: 'offscreen.html',
  reasons: ['BLOBS'],
  justification: 'Assemble downloaded video segments into one file',
});

The offscreen page downloads the segments, remuxes them, creates a blob: URL and messages it back; the service worker then calls chrome.downloads.download({ url: blobUrl }).

4. Remuxing in the browser with mux.js

mux.js transmuxes MPEG-TS into fragmented MP4 in plain JS. No ffmpeg.wasm, no 25 MB download. Feed it segments in order; it emits an init segment plus media fragments you can concatenate. When audio is a separate rendition, transmux both and interleave by timestamp.

5. Big lessons and memory: write to OPFS

A two-hour 1080p lesson can be over a gigabyte. Instead of keeping every chunk in RAM, I stream remuxed output into the Origin Private File System and build the final Blob from the file:

const root = await navigator.storage.getDirectory();
const fh = await root.getFileHandle(tempName, { create: true });
const w = await fh.createWritable();
// for each remuxed chunk: await w.write(chunk);
await w.close();
const file = await fh.getFile();          // a Blob backed by disk

Delete the temp file once chrome.downloads reports complete, and also on cancel.

6. Cancel has to cancel everything

Users click "stop". That has to abort in-flight fetches (one AbortController per job), tell the offscreen document to drop its job, cancel the chrome.downloads item if it already started, and delete the OPFS temp file. Otherwise you leak half-written gigabyte files.

7. Firefox: no offscreen documents

Firefox runs MV3 backgrounds as event pages and has no chrome.offscreen. My port loads the offscreen script directly into the background page and replaces the runtime messages with direct function calls, plus a tiny keep-alive while a job runs. Firefox's webRequest also has no initiator, so use originUrl / documentUrl instead.

Result

The extension is called Keep My Course. It does this for Skool lessons (native player and Loom embeds), adds a searchable transcript from the captions, and everything runs locally: nothing is uploaded.

If you're fighting HLS in an extension, I'm happy to answer questions in the comments. And if you see a better way to handle separate audio renditions, I'd love to hear it.

Earlier I wrote about the user side of this, why right-click "Save video as" doesn't work on Skool.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of Keep My Course.

articles.title: Running Real-ESRGAN in the browser: ONNX Runtime Web, WebGPU, and tiles without seams
articles.description: I wanted an image upscaler that runs entirely in the browser: no upload, no API key, works on a...
articles.body_html:
I wanted an image upscaler that runs entirely in the browser: no upload, no API key, works on a phone. This post covers what it took to get Real-ESRGAN running on ONNX Runtime Web with WebGPU and a WebAssembly fallback, and the few details that made the difference between "works on my laptop" and "works on any photo".

The result is live at cv.cm/en/image-upscaler if you want to try it before reading.

Picking a model that fits in a tab

My first attempt used Swin2SR. Quality was fine, but on WebGPU it took seconds per 192 px tile. A 12-megapixel phone photo is a few hundred tiles, so that was a non-starter.

Real-ESRGAN ships two "compact" models (realesr-general-x4v3 for photos and realesr-animevideov3 for anime and line art) built on SRVGGNetCompact. That network is a plain stack of 3×3 convolutions with PReLU, then a PixelShuffle, plus a nearest-neighbour upsample of the input added back as a residual:

  • photo model: 32 conv layers, about 1.2M parameters
  • anime model: 16 conv layers, about 0.6M parameters

On WebGPU a tile runs in tens of milliseconds. The download is small too:

Model fp32 fp16
photo (general-x4v3) 4.9 MB 2.4 MB
anime (animevideov3) 2.5 MB 1.3 MB

Exporting to ONNX

The released .pth files load straight into a small re-implementation of the architecture (same layer layout, so load_state_dict just works). The export needs dynamic height and width so one model handles any tile size:

torch.onnx.export(
    model, torch.rand(1, 3, 64, 64), "model.onnx",
    input_names=["pixel_values"], output_names=["reconstruction"],
    dynamic_axes={
        "pixel_values": {2: "height", 3: "width"},
        "reconstruction": {2: "out_height", 3: "out_width"},
    },
    opset_version=17,
)

# fp16 weights, but keep float32 inputs and outputs so the JS side never changes
fp16 = float16.convert_float_to_float16(onnx.load("model.onnx"), keep_io_types=True)
onnx.save(fp16, "model_fp16.onnx")

keep_io_types=True matters: the browser code always feeds a Float32Array and reads one back, whichever file it loaded. The export script also runs both ONNX files through onnxruntime on the CPU against the PyTorch output on a random 96×80 input, so a bad conversion fails loudly instead of producing slightly wrong colours.

Choosing the backend

The worker picks one of three variants once:

async function detectBackend(nav: WorkerNavigator): Promise<"gpu16" | "gpu" | "cpu"> {
  const gpu = (nav as any).gpu;
  if (!gpu) return "cpu";
  try {
    const adapter = await gpu.requestAdapter({ powerPreference: "high-performance" });
    if (!adapter) return "cpu";
    return adapter.features.has("shader-f16") ? "gpu16" : "gpu";
  } catch {
    return "cpu";
  }
}
  • gpu16: WebGPU with the fp16 model (half the download)
  • gpu: WebGPU with fp32 when the adapter has no shader-f16
  • cpu: the wasm execution provider with the fp32 model

The WebAssembly path is only reasonable with threads, and threads need SharedArrayBuffer, which needs cross-origin isolation. The AI pages are served with COOP and COEP: credentialless, and the thread count leaves room for the page:

const cores = navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 4;
ort.env.wasm.numThreads = self.crossOriginIsolated ? Math.max(1, Math.min(8, cores - 2)) : 1;

The model bytes go through the Cache API, so the second visit doesn't download anything.

Tiles without seams

Running a 4000×3000 image in one go would need a 16000×12000 float output, which is about 2.3 GB for three channels. So the image is processed in tiles: 384 px on the GPU and 192 px on the CPU.

Naive tiling leaves visible seams, because pixels at a tile's edge don't see their neighbours. The fix is to feed each tile with 24 px of context on every side (wider than the network's receptive field), then write back only the core:

const SR_PAD = 24;
const ax = Math.max(0, x0 - SR_PAD);           // padded tile origin
const ay = Math.max(0, y0 - SR_PAD);
const tw = Math.min(w, x1 + SR_PAD) - ax;      // padded tile size
const th = Math.min(h, y1 + SR_PAD) - ay;
// ... run the model on [ax, ay, tw, th], then copy only
// [(x0 - ax) * 4, (x1 - ax) * 4) × [(y0 - ay) * 4, (y1 - ay) * 4) into the output

Because the model has dynamic axes, edge tiles that are smaller than 384 px need no special handling.

2× from a 4× model, without ever building the 4× image

Both models are ×4 only. For a 2× result, the obvious approach is to upscale ×4 and then resize down, but that briefly holds the full ×4 image in memory.

Instead, each 4×4 block of model output is averaged into a 2×2 block while the tile is being written. The full ×4 image never exists, and averaging is also a decent downscale filter:

const shrink = 4 / scale;   // 1 for ×4, 2 for ×2
for (let dy = 0; dy < shrink; dy++)
  for (let dx = 0; dx < shrink; dx++) {
    const si = (y * shrink + dy) * RW + x * shrink + dx;
    red += r[si]; green += r[rp + si]; blue += r[2 * rp + si];
  }
const n = 255 / (shrink * shrink);
out[di] = red * n; out[di + 1] = green * n; out[di + 2] = blue * n;

The output buffer itself is capped at 16 megapixels. Larger requests are scaled down to fit before upscaling, so a phone doesn't run out of memory halfway through.

What I'd tell someone doing the same

  • Pick the architecture for the runtime, not for the leaderboard. A plain conv stack maps well to WebGPU; a transformer with window attention did not, at least for me.
  • Ship fp16 only where the GPU says it can run it. shader-f16 is the switch; keep IO in fp32 so the JS doesn't branch.
  • Pad tiles by more than the receptive field and crop back. It's a few lines and removes every seam.
  • Test the export numerically, not just "it loads".

Everything runs in a module worker, and the image never leaves the device. The same setup (WebGPU first, threaded WASM otherwise, models from the Cache API) also runs a depth-map generator and background removal in the same toolkit at cv.cm. Questions about the export or the tiling are welcome in the comments.

articles.body_html:
I recently built a small personality quiz about the seven heavenly virtues: 35 statements, five per virtue, and a score out of 100 for each one at the end. The site is plain Astro with no backend, and I wanted the result to look like something from a cathedral rather than a dashboard. So instead of a radar chart library, the result is drawn as a seven-light rose window, where each pane of glass fills from the centre outward in proportion to its score.

Here are the three pieces that made it work, with the real code.

1. Scoring with reversed statements

Some statements describe the virtue ("When I'm praised, I mention the people who helped") and some describe the sin against it. Sin statements are reverse-scored, so agreeing with everything doesn't inflate the result. Each virtue has n answers of 1 to 5, which gives a range of n to 5n, mapped onto 0–100:

function score(questions: Question[], answers: number[]): number[] {
  const sums = new Map(virtues.map((v) => [v.id, 0]));
  const counts = new Map(virtues.map((v) => [v.id, 0]));
  questions.forEach((q, i) => {
    const raw = answers[i] ?? 3;
    const val = q.reverse ? 6 - raw : raw;
    sums.set(q.virtue, (sums.get(q.virtue) ?? 0) + val);
    counts.set(q.virtue, (counts.get(q.virtue) ?? 0) + 1);
  });
  return virtues.map((v) => {
    const n = counts.get(v.id) || 1;
    return Math.round((((sums.get(v.id) ?? 3 * n) - n) / (4 * n)) * 100);
  });
}

Because it divides by the count per virtue, the same function also scores a 14-question quick version (two statements per virtue) without any changes.

2. Shareable results with no database

There's no server to store results, so the seven scores go into the URL as two-digit pairs:

// ?r=72558190436067
function encode(scores: number[]) {
  return scores.map((s) => String(Math.min(99, s)).padStart(2, '0')).join('');
}

function decode(r: string | null): number[] | null {
  if (!r || !/^\d{14}$/.test(r)) return null;
  return Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => Number(r.slice(i * 2, i * 2 + 2)));
}

A perfect 100 is stored as 99 to keep every pair two digits. When the page loads with a valid ?r=, it renders the result directly and switches the wording from "your" to "their", so a shared link reads as a friend's result instead of yours. Answers never leave the browser.

3. The rose window

The window is a string of SVG built in a few lines of trigonometry. Each light is a pointed lancet drawn once, pointing straight up, and then rotated into place:

const N = 7;
const R_IN = 33;      // where the lancets start
const R_SPRING = 66;  // where the pointed arch springs
const R_TIP = 88;     // apex of the arch
const HALF_ANGLE = (22 * Math.PI) / 180;

const lancet = (() => {
  const t = Math.tan(HALF_ANGLE);
  const xi = R_IN * t;
  const xs = R_SPRING * t;
  const arc = 30;
  return `M${-xi} ${-R_IN}L${-xs} ${-R_SPRING}` +
    `A${arc} ${arc} 0 0 1 0 ${-R_TIP}` +
    `A${arc} ${arc} 0 0 1 ${xs} ${-R_SPRING}` +
    `L${xi} ${-R_IN}A${R_IN} ${R_IN} 0 0 0 ${-xi} ${-R_IN}Z`;
})();

Two circular arcs meeting at the tip give the Gothic point. To turn the window into a chart, each pane is first filled with its colour at 17% opacity (unlit glass), then a full-strength circle centred on the boss is clipped to the lancet's shape:

const reach = R_IN + (R_TIP - R_IN) * Math.max(score, 0.03);
// inside the rotated <g> for light i:
`<clipPath id="c${i}"><use href="#lancet"/></clipPath>`
`<use href="#lancet" fill="${colour}" fill-opacity=".17"/>`
`<g clip-path="url(#c${i})"><circle r="${reach}" fill="${colour}"/></g>`

A score of 0.4 lights the inner 40% of the pane; the rest stays dim. Because the lit edge is part of a circle around the centre, all seven fills line up like rings on a radar chart. With the virtue names written around the rim, it reads as one without looking like one.

Because it's just a string dropped into innerHTML, there's no chart library to ship, and leaving out scores draws the same window with every light fully lit.

Bonus: one canvas gotcha

The share cards are 1080 × 1920 PNGs drawn on a canvas, with the top virtue's painting as the background. The obvious move is to await img.decode() before drawing, but on large images decode() can stay pending indefinitely in some browsers, and the card never appears. Waiting on the plain load event avoids it:

const img = new Image();
img.onload = () => resolve(img);
img.onerror = () => reject(new Error(`could not load ${id}`));
img.src = `/art/card/${id}.png`;

If you want to see the window lit up with your own scores, the quiz is live at 7virtuestest.org. It takes about five minutes, and the result link it gives you is just those fourteen digits.

articles.title: We made a multiplayer browser game with no game server
articles.description: A peer-to-peer PvP game on a static site, using Trystero, WebRTC and Nostr relays. Here's how it works and where it breaks.
articles.body_html:
Super Nova Arena is a small PvP game that runs in a browser tab. Your mouse is your player, a glowing star. Pull back, let go, and you sling a shot at someone else. Space puts up a shield, right click (or Q) drops a mine, and after 90 seconds whoever has the most KOs wins. Up to 8 people can share a lobby.

The part I actually want to talk about is the plumbing, because there isn't any. No game server, no backend at all. The site is a static page on GitHub Pages and players connect straight to each other.

How the connecting works

We use Trystero with its Nostr strategy. Public Nostr relays only help peers find each other, and once they have, everything goes over WebRTC directly between players.

For the lobby list, everyone joins one shared room called lobby-index, and each person advertises which lobby they're in through their user state. Every lobby is its own room, capped at 8. Inside a lobby there are three things going on: each player's state (name, color, health, KOs, downs, wins, whether they're dead), an event channel for shots, mines, shields and hits, and one shared match object for the round.

A round goes waiting, countdown, live, over, then around again. The bit I like is that every transition is tied to the round number, so any player can push it forward and it doesn't matter if two of them do it at the same moment. There's no host to lose. Everything coming in from other players gets validated and rate-limited, since we can't trust anybody.

The rest of it

It's one index.html. CSS and JS are inline, no framework, no build step. The only outside code is two vendored modules that load when needed: Trystero when someone opens the lobby panel, and modern-screenshot when someone sends a bug report with a screenshot.

Physics runs on a fixed 1/120 second step on a virtual 1600x900 table that gets stretched to fit your screen. Other players' positions are smoothed between updates so they don't jitter around. For the slingshot you stand still, press to plant, pull back (up to 330 units) and let go. A full pull does 2 damage.

Rendering has a couple of tricks. The nebula clouds are drawn on an offscreen layer at 0.45 resolution. The page also checks your monitor's refresh rate and only draws every Nth frame to land near 60 FPS, so 60 and 120 Hz screens run at 60 and a 144 Hz screen settles at a steady 72. If it's still slow, it drops to 1x pixel density.

Where it falls apart

  • Each player decides for themselves whether they got hit. That kept things simple, but it means cheating is easy.
  • There's no TURN server, so some strict networks just can't connect.
  • Everyone in a lobby can see everyone else's IP address. The lobby panel says so, but still.

Come break it

If you've built peer-to-peer netcode before, I'd love to hear what's going to bite us later. Or just play it at flirtworks.co. Practice vs bots works if nobody's around, which, this early, is most of the time. It's early access, so there's a Bug button at the top right that sends reports straight to our Discord.

articles.title: Finding the blanks in a PDF form with nothing but pixels
articles.description: Most PDF forms people deal with are flat: a scan, or a Word document exported to PDF with Name:...
articles.body_html:
Most PDF forms people deal with are flat: a scan, or a Word document exported to PDF with Name: ________ lines. To make one fillable you have to place a text box over every blank, by hand. Acrobat's "Prepare Form" does this automatically, and I wanted the same thing in the browser for KaiPDF, where files never leave the device.

The trick I ended up with ignores the PDF's structure completely. It renders each page to pixels and looks for the shapes a person looks for: a line with empty space above it, an empty box, a small square. That means it works the same on scans as on born-digital PDFs.

Here's how it works, in about 200 lines of TypeScript.

1. Render and threshold

The page is rendered with PDFium (compiled to WebAssembly) at about 2 px per point, then turned into a 1-bit "ink" map:

const dark = new Uint8Array(width * height);
for (let i = 0, j = 0; j < dark.length; i += 4, j++) {
  const a = px[i + 3] / 255;
  const lum = (0.299 * px[i] + 0.587 * px[i + 1] + 0.114 * px[i + 2]) * a + 255 * (1 - a);
  dark[j] = lum < 150 ? 1 : 0;
}

2. Horizontal strokes

Scan each row for dark runs at least 6 pt long. A printed line is usually 1 to 3 pixels thick, so a run in one row is joined to a run in the next row when both ends line up within 2 px. Keeping only the strokes that touched the previous row makes this linear instead of quadratic, which matters on text-heavy pages:

let open: Seg[] = [];
for (let y = 0; y < height; y++) {
  const next: Seg[] = [];
  // ...for each dark run [x0, x1] in this row:
  const s = open.find((g) => Math.abs(x0 - g.x0) <= 2 && Math.abs(x1 - g.x1) <= 2);
  if (s) { s.y1 = y; next.push(s); } else { /* start a new stroke */ }
  open = next;
}

Anything thicker than ~2 pt is a filled area or bold text, not a stroke, and is dropped.

3. Boxes, table rows and tick boxes

Two strokes with the same span, a few points apart, are a box if both ends are joined by vertical ink. Checking a column is a cheap vote: what fraction of pixels between the strokes are dark (with ±2 px of tolerance for anti-aliasing).

A table row is just a wide box, so before accepting it, I look for interior columns that are dark top to bottom and cut the row into cells. Each cell is then checked for ink on its own. Header cells contain text, so they are skipped, and empty cells become fields. A box that is small and square (under ~22 pt) becomes a checkbox.

4. Answer lines

A stroke that isn't part of a box is a candidate answer line, like Name: ________. The test that separates it from underlined text is the space above it: grow a rectangle upwards in 2 pt steps while it stays almost empty (<1.5% ink). If at least 9 pt of empty space sits above the line, it's a blank waiting for an answer. Otherwise text sits on it and it's an underline.

5. Naming the fields

A field named "Text 7" is useless to whoever collects the answers. PDFium gives the page's text lines with positions, so each field takes its name from:

  • text on the same row that ends just before it (Date of birth: ____ → "Date of birth"),
  • otherwise text just above it, overlapping horizontally,
  • for tick boxes, the text just to the right ("☐ Student" → "Student").

Trailing colons and underscores are trimmed. Cells in a table column inherit the column heading and get numbered: "Club 1", "Club 2".

Results

On a test membership form (labelled blanks, three tick boxes, a comments box and a three-column table) it found all 17 answer spaces and named every one correctly. It misses things on skewed scans, so the editor lets you drag fields on, snap them to each other and rename them. Then pdf-lib writes real AcroForm fields that work in Acrobat Reader, Chrome, Edge and Firefox.

The pixel approach is crude compared to a layout model, but it costs nothing to run, needs no upload and handles scans for free. You can try it on your own form: Make PDF Fillable. If you'd rather start from scratch, the same site has a form designer with templates.

I'd love to hear about forms it gets wrong.

articles.title: HSC ICT Number System: Binary to Decimal in 30 Seconds — Without Memorizing Tables
articles.description: HSC ICT students in Bangladesh lose easy marks on number-system questions every year — not because...
articles.body_html:
HSC ICT students in Bangladesh lose easy marks on number-system questions every year — not because the topic is hard, but because they try to memorize conversion tables. There is a simpler way: understand place value once, and every conversion becomes the same small calculation.

The one idea: place value

In decimal, 25 means 2 tens + 5 ones: 2×10 + 5×1. Binary works exactly the same way, only the base is 2 instead of 10. Each position is worth twice the one before it: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...

So binary 1010 means: 1×8 + 0×4 + 1×2 + 0×1 = 8 + 2 = 10 in decimal.

Binary to decimal — the 30-second method

Write the place values above the digits, multiply, add:

  1   0   1   1
  8   4   2   1
= 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11

So binary 1011 = 11 in decimal. That is the whole method — no table to memorize.
